Mr. J. T. THORSON (Winnipeg South Centre) presented the second and final report of the special committee appointed to consider the question of the adequacy of the remuneration paid to the judges of the various courts in Canada, as follows:
The special committee appointed to consider the question of the adequacy of the remuneration paid to the judges of the various courts in Canada beg leave to present the following as their second and final report:
Your committee, composed of fifteen members, were appointed on April 15, 1928, in accordance with a resolution passed in the house on March 20, 1928, and were empowered to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time, and were further empowered on April 19, 1928, to print their minutes of proceedings and any evidence taken by them, and to sit while the house is in session.
Your committee met for organization on April 19, 1928, and since then have held seven sessions and heard twenty witnesses. Representations were also made to your committee by letters and telegrams from numerous persons who did not appear before them. Your committee also had before them reports of committees of the county courts judges and of the Canadian Bar Association, resolutions from various organizations and information from the Department of Justice and the Bureau of Statistics.
Your committee gave careful consideration to the question referred to them and find that the remuneration paid to the judges in the various courts in Canada as hereinafter mentioned is inadequate and ought to be increased.
Your committee, therefore, recommend:
1.	That the salaries of the judges of the district and county courts of the various provinces of Canada be increased by $2,000 per annum each.
2.	That the salaries of the judges of the superior courts of the various provinces of Canada, and of the Exchequer Court of Canada be increased by $2,000 per annum each.
56103-I97J
3.	That the salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada be increased by $3,000 per annum each.
A printed copy of the committee's minutes of proceedings and evidence is herewith submitted for the information of the house.
All of which is respectfully submitted.
J. T. Thosson,
Chairman.

On the orders of the day:

There is a matter to which I wish to direct the attention of the government. It may possibly be slightly out of order, but seeing that the discussion of it is in the interest of the people

Deceptive Mining Literature
generally and does not constitute any criticism of the government, I do not think any objection will be taken to my bringing it up at this stage. There have been passing through the mails in the	past two or	three	yearsvarious tipster sheets on mining stocks and things of that sort. The other day I was handed a copy of one publication which entered the country freely last year-the Financialistic Debater published in Boston, the editor being one E. T. Morton. This sheet specializes in what are called "mystery stocks," and it is purely a fake, a crooked effort to steal the money of the people of Canada, and also of the people of the United States, for that	matter.	Of	course thepeople of the United States can look after themselves;	but I	think	some	effortshould be made by the government, through the Post Office Department, to prevent a sheet of this kind from going through the mails. Last year this same paper, published, I believe,	by the	same	man,	came
through the mails in large numbers, describing the prospects of so-called "mystery stocks" and holding out the most extravagant promises, most, if not all, of which were proved later by Toronto Saturday Night and other papers to be complete fakes and nothing but a method of wheedling money out of the people. I have no doubt they succeeded in securing a good deal of money from the people of this country, because as we all know many people are gullible when it comes to promises of sudden wealth. I do not know that this publication has ever been barred from the mails, but at that time it was shown to be crooked. The other day I was handed this particular copy I have in my hand, it having been sent to someone in Ottawa. I had intended taking the matter up on the estimates of the Post Office Department, but I thought we might as well dispose of it now so as to afford the government an earlier opportunity to try to deal with the situation. It is true that the publisher has cut down the size of the sheet; it now comes through the mails more in the form of a letter than of a circular. It may therefore be harder to get at. But on the envelope containing the copy which I hold in my hand, there is printed the name of the editor, "E. T. Morton, Unity building, Boston, Massachusetts". I know the government is just as anxious as I am to see to it that the people of Canada shall not be cheated out of their money. It is difficult enough for us to raise money here for the development of our own resources as well as, to a certain extent at least, for the purpose of appeasing the gambling instinct we all possess. There is hope for some return from various mining 
propositions in Canada, but there is no hope for any return of money sunk in the schemes advertised by the Financialistic Debater. I appeal to the government to put a stop to the carriage of such sheets through our mails.

In reply to my hon. friend I would say that my attention was drawn to this publication or to a similar one a couple of weeks ago, and instructions were given to have the matter looked into in order to see what could be done. It is hard to detect these letters now that they are being sent in envelopes, but since my hon. friend has stated that the name appears on the envelope we may be able to do something. Would my hon. friend let me have that letter?

Yes, and I would like to
draw the attention of the minister to the fact that on this envelope at least, and I presume on most of the envelopes containing these letters, the name is on the outside, and I presume it will be there until these people see what action is taken by this government. As I have said, this' concern have been shown by the Toronto Saturday Night and other financial papers to be fakers, and I think something should be done to put an end to their activities.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext: A day or two ago the Prime Minister was asked a question with regard to the Kellogg peace proposal. I see that the House of Lords have declared themselves in favour of that proposal, but the British government have taken the ground that they cannot act until the dominions are heard from. I wonder if it would not be possible for Canada to express an opinion shortly with regard to this matter?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MULTILATERAL TREATY PROPOSED BY THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
From what my hon. friend has just said there would appear to be an erroneous impression with regard to the attitude of the British government, if it is thought that the British government cannot act until the governments of the dominions have been heard from. I understand that the government of Great Britain have expressed the view, and certainly it has been so expressed in the House of Lords, that they arc prepared to become a party to the treaty.

Pension Act-Mr. Geary
As I understand the matter, the United States extended an invitation to the four great powers in the first instance to ascertain whether or not they would become parties to the treaty. The United States took this action before extending a similar invitation to other countries or to any of the British dominions. Now that the British government have expressed their intention of becoming a party to the treaty, I have not the least doubt that Canada also, along with the other dominions, will be asked to become a party to the treaty, and I have no doubt also that when we are asked it will be the wish of this country that we should become a party to it. At the moment, as far as any invitation is concerned, it is a matter which is receiving attention, and we may expect to be in a position to make an announcement shortly.

Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Health) moved the third reading of Bill No. 289, to amend the Pension Act.

I do not propose to take up more than a few minutes of the time of the house in connection with one particular section of the bill now under consideration; I refer to section
5.	This section was not passed upon and brought to this house by the committee considering this question, but was inserted by the government. Just in passing I would like to say that from what one can hear each individual member of that committee may take to himself the gratitude of a great many returned men, and of course I include in that committee the minister himself. The returned soldiers are grateful for the assiduous manner in which the committee carried out its duties and for the thorough way in which the problems of the returned soldiers were dealt with and solutions recommended to this house. That committee functioned particularly well under the very sympathetic chairmanship of my gallant and honourable friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power).
The section which was inserted by the government however is a retrograde step, I venture to say. I presented my reasons for this statement a short time ago and do not propose to take up the time of the house by repeating them. Section 5 of this bill repeals sections 4 to 8 inclusive of the present act, and substitutes three other sections therefor. Section 4, which it is proposed to repeal, is as follows:
The commission shall be provided with suitable offices at the city of Ottawa for the commissioners and for the officers and employees of the commission, such branch offices elsewhere as may be required and all necessary furnishings, stationery and equipment for the conduct, maintenance, and performance of the duties of the commission.

Pension AcL-Mr. Geary
Thus the pension commission not only had separate, independent quarters, but also had its own staff and functioned as an independent body. There is no provision in this proposed amendment for the accommodation of the commission and nothing is said which would indicate that it is to have its own staff. Instead of that, it will have to depend upon such assistance as may be given by a department of the government, the department headed by my friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health. Section 5, which it is proposed to repeal, is as follows:
The commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil Service Act.
2. The salaries and other remuneration of the officers, clerks and employees of the commission, and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of this act, shall be paid out of moneys to be provided by parliament.
This section is to disappear entirely; the commission will no longer be a deputy head, and if one turns to the Civil Service Act it is easy to see how far-reaching this change really is. Under the Civil Service Act it is the deputy head who organizes the particular branch under him and provides in a general way for appointments, for remuneration, for duties and so on. It strikes me particularly with regard to this section that we are not maintaining the independence of the board of pension commissioners but rather that we are striking at that independence in causing the board to be attached for all purposes to a political department of the government. As I have indicated, this is a matter which has attracted the attention of the officials of various soldier organizations, and which is abhorrent to them. They see that this commission is likely to drift more and more into politics and further and further aw:ay from that independence which has been so important in the minds of those who have had to depend upon the board. Pensions should be kept out of politics and should be looked after by a body which is independent and subject to no dictation from or leading by a department of the government. I take it that under the existing act we are functioning in the right way with regard to pensions, but if we let pensions drift into politics in any way we are not carrying on in the proper manner. We do not know how far the removal of the status as deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil Service Act may go, but it will go a long way. If you run through the provisions of that act you will see how much its operation depends upon the fact that the spokesman for the department is treated as a deputy head. The Board

of Railway Commissioners is a deputy head under the Civil Service Act. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is not the proper method to engage men to give the attention that should be given to pensions, and then place them under the management and jurisdiction of a department of the government.
The government had a report from Mr. G. W. Scott in October, 1927, and Mr. Scott was asked to make that report because there were certain unsatisfactory conditions with regard to the administration of pensions. Among other things, Mr. Scott recommended that the board of pension commissioners should be given such a staff of medioal examiners, investigators and clerks as would enable them to function as an independent body for the purpose of collecting all necessary information and evidence relating to matters relevant to eligibility of ex-service men and their dependents for pensions, rendering decisions thereon, and calculating the pensions payable. I submit that this suggested amendment of the government goes entirely contrary to that very carefully considered opinion and recommendation of Mr. Scott. We are ignoring those recommendations and going in the opposite direction. It seems to me that the full investigation that Mr. Scott gave the matter is entitled to consideration. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I beg to move, seconded by M|r. Casselman, that in effect old section 5 be re-enacted, or left in the statute. My motion will read:
That the said hill be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole with instructions that they have power to add thereto the following sections :
"The commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil Service Act."
And	.
"The salaries and other remuneration of the officers, clerks and employees of the commission. and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of this act shall be paid out of moneys to be provided by parliament."
This would make it similar to the method in which the railway board gets its money. The railway board is a deputy head, and is independent. I say that the moneys of this commission should be paid by parliament and the commission should be in the position of a deputy head of a department.
One result of the proposed amendment that will be seen at once with relation to medical researches, history reporting, and consideration of questions affecting pensions, will be that these matters will be handled, not necessarily as they have been heretofore under the pension commissioners, but may be done by some official of the department. Under this section,

Pension Act-Mr. King (Kootenay)
the sole remaining duty of the pension commissioners may be simply adjudicating upon evidence which will be handed to them by a department of the government, which department is not likely to be any freer from political suggestion than any other department of the government.
Will the hon. member allow me to ask a question? Of what department would you make this commission a deputy head?

That does not matter. The deputy head of a department is a person through whom the Civil Service Commission function or collaborate regarding appointments. The Board of Railway Commissioners is a deputy head of a department, but it is not a deputy head of the Department of Railways and Canals.
Not all of them.

All but this small section in Ottawa. All the doctors, and outside investigators, except the small staff in Ottawa, were brought within the control of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. I stated the other day that I thought a mistake or an error in judgment had been made at that time, in that the medical service and the investigators carrying on investigations into pension matters should be under the control of the pension board. That is what we are doing in the department to-day.
Following the Scott report, an agreement was entered into with the pension commissioners whereby they would have their medical representatives, one or two or three, whatever they considered necessary, in each of the units. If at times it was found that they required extra assistance in any unit, they merely asked the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-estaiblisfhment for that assistance, and representatives were detailed from that department to do their work. Those representatives then reported directly to the commission on the matter which they had under consideration.
We do not propose to interfere with the stenographic and clerical staff, but we do think that it is advantageous, and it will be in the interests of economy, that that staff should be paid through our central auditing and [accounting board. We are making large savings in reorganizing in this way, and there cannot be any reasonable ground for contending that there should be another staff, with all that goes with a comparatively large staff, to take care of pay and accounting in the same building and under the same conditions.
Personally, I do not see any reas'on why this section should be amended. The section is broad enough, and it covers the activities of the department in the case of the relationship that exists between the pension board and the department, and puts in the form of a statute conditions that have existed by regulations heretofore.

Would the amendment as moved by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) interfere with the operation of the act; that is', if this amendment were passed would it hamper in any way the carrying into effect of any important section of the bill before the house?

I do not know that it would interfere, but it has been the practice, irespective of what my hon. friend has said regarding the railway commission. When this matter was under consideration last week, I was surprised to learn that the railway commission did not act as a deputy head. They are under the Department of Railways, and they act as a judicial body, just as this body will act independently of the department in judicial matters which they have to consider.
The pension commissioners will be working under very much better .conditions. The medical officers, upon whom they will depend for the knowledge obtained regarding pensioners, will be under their, own control. They will be in a much more independent and better position than they have been heretofore. I see no reason why we should amend the section, as my hon. friend wished to do. At this time I compliment the chairman and the members of the special committee upon their diligence and the thoroughness of their work in amending the present act and I believe these amendments will result in better conditions in regard to those who are interested in pension matters.
3112	COMMONS
Pension Act-Mr. King (Kootenay)

I cannot see
any advantage in it. We have amalgamated two departments of government and we have now one deputy head. The pension commission is attached to that department. It has always been attached to one department and it must so be attached. The commissioners will make their requests to the deputy head and those requests will come to the minister in the ordinary way. I cannot see any advantage in lumbering up the bill by including that section. Sections 4 to 8 have been redrafted under the new section and anyone reading those sections carefully and reading the new section will find this a much better draftsmanship. The matter is more clearly expressed than in the wandering sections we had before.

I quite agree with
the minister as to the redrafting of those sections. In the bill now before the house the matter is expressed more dearly and in much better language. In effect it puts in a better way what is really the law except as to the omission of subsections 1 and 2 of section 5. By the omission of those subsections the effect of the law is changed. Power is taken away from the pension commissioners. If it is desirable to lessen their powers, well and good, but it does not seem to me well to do so. The minister must have changed his mind somewhat on this subject since the 14th of this month. Then both the Minister of Health and the Minister of National Defence were quite of opinion that those subsections should be left in. If the minister will pardon me for quoting him I will quote from Hansard of May 14, at page 2970, where he is reported as saying:
Or we could insert the old section, which says:
"The commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purposes of the Civil Service Act."
Then follow some remarks by the leader of the opposition to which the minister assented. Following that the leader of the opposition said:
Under those circumstances, I think the minister's suggestion would meet the case.

That is the suggestion of the minister himself that that subsection be left in and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) said:
We can reinsert the old section.
It was understood that would be done. Why has a change been made?

It was understood in this way. A discussion was going on and I advised the committee that I would' withhold the section and make further inquiries. It appeared to me while I was in my seat that we might reinsert that section, but after inquiry and consideration I advised the committee the next day that we did not think the new section should be amended and the old section reinserted. That is the way the matter stands. I have nothing more to say. The bill has had very careful consideration by the committee and I see no advantage in having the section amended as has been suggested.

I
think the minister's first thought was the correct one, namely, that the section ought to be re-inserted in this legislation. The minister when speaking a few minutes ago said that he thought the provisions of the new section placed the pension commissioners in a more independent and better position than they are in at present. I take an altogether different view of the matter. It seems to me that the new section is drafted for the purpose of putting the pension commission 5n a subordinate position to what they were in before. As far as my experience goes the pension commission has been one of the outstanding commissions that we have had of late years in the Dominion. Its work has been well done. The head of the commission is a man with a splendid war record who understands the needs and feelings of the returned soldiers fully as well as anybody can in this country. Now an effort is being made to rob that commission of a certain amount of their standing and position and to make them simply a branch of the Department of Soldiers' Reestablishment. That is my understanding of this section. The minister said that the pension commission has always been attached to that department.
Since 1920.

It was attached
to that department in 1920. That is correct, but its independent power still remains with the commission under the sections of the old act which the minister now proposes to strike

Pension Act-Sir George Perley
out. Under subsection 5 of section 5 the head of the commission was given all the powers and duties of a deputy head of the department for the purposes of the Civil Service Act and any moneys provided for the purpose of carrying out the work of the commission are provided by parliament itself and not simply as a branch of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Reestablishment. The minister has commented with regard to the railway commission and the fact that they are attached to the Department of Railways and Canals. But the railway commission occupies a special place by itself and the railway commissioners have positions peculiar to their own office. There is in this country no other position, saving that of the Prime Minister himself, higher than that of the chairman of the railway commission. The commissioners have most onerous duties to perform; they are the people's court for many questions, and the chairman and members of the railway commission have a special place assigned to them in the social and public life of the Dominion.
This section that the minister proposes to strike out gives the head of the pension commission the rank of a deputy head. Parliament has given a similar rank to many positions outside of the actual deputy ministers themselves. Now the minister wishes to alter the position of the pension commission. He deliberately says so; by this section as I read it-and if I am wrong the minister will correct me-he undertakes to make the pension commission simply a branch of his department subject to instructions from himself and his deputy head as well. That is not, as I understand the matter, what is wanted by the people or the returned soldiers. The pension commission has been an independent, well-managed commission, absolutely apart from anything political. There is no department of government that can at all times be entirely independent of politics. The minister knows that himself; he is subject to all sorts of influences which he cannot always ignore from his friends and supporters. The pension commission has been doing its work faithfully and well.
Mr. KING (Kootenay); Under the Pension Act and it will continue to do so.

Under the Pension Act and the pension commission has had an independent position which is being taken away from it by this legislation. He says:
The commission shall from time to time make such reports to the minister as he may direct.
As he may direct. I submit that the pension commission knows better how to make its own reports than the minister himself can possibly know.

Read the old
section.

It says:
The commission shall furnish the minister with such reports, statements and information as he may at any time require.
Now which is the better section?

I am going
through the whole of the changes. I admit that some of the wording is a great deal better in the new sections, but the effect of this change is to take away from the pension board the independent position which it has occupied under the old act, and I do not think the minister can deny that. If that is his purpose, I submit that the first thought that he had the other day when this matter was under discussion was the correct one, and I think this amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) covers the point admirably. There is no effort made to alter the wording of the proposed new sections whatever, and I agree with the hon. member for South Toronto that the position of the pension board should be maintained intact as it is now; that it should be practically an independent board' to consider all these questions under the law without any political favour or influence being brought to bear on them, and attached to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, but not under that department, as it is the minister's purpose to make it. As I read it, the deliberate intention of this section is to rob the pension board of its independent position and to make it subordinate to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. They were always attached to the department, and1 they were under the minister in a sense, and I am sure they always took cognizance of the advice of the minister, but at the same time they were not subject to any political influence whatever, while the minister cannot escape being subject to it. He may at times be strong enough to resist that pressure, but at other times he will find himself unable to do so, and I submit to him that, without changing the wording of this section, he should agree to the amendment which has been moved by the hon. member for South
Pension Act-Mr. Power

Toronto, which simply restores one of the clauses of the present act, which says:
The commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil* Service Act.
That preserves the position and independence of the commission. I do not think it is fair for the minister to undertake in this way to place the pension commission under his authority and that of his deputy minister, and to take away from them the independent position which they have always occupied under the act, in which position they have given such great and valuable service to the people of this country.

I
must confess, Mr. Speaker, that I have not given much thought to the amendment which has just been proposed by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary), nor can I see that his amendment would change very much what is in the act at present, but being proposed by the hon. gentleman, it must mean something, for I know him well enough to know that he would not waste his time and that of the house by making a suggestion which did not mean anything. I have been trying for the past few moments to understand just what the objection is to the section as brought down by the minister. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Sir George Perley) has made reference to the social position of a deputy head. If that is the only reason why we should keep the old section in, I think we are wasting the time of the house in discussing it.

Not only his
social but his official position.
What is the meaning of his official position?

The position he
occupies as regards the other officers in the department.

I am free to confess that
I do not understand what that means either. The position which he occupies as regards other officers in the department? I assume that he is the head of the pensions board, whether he be called a deputy head or not, and that as such he would have under his control the officers of the pension board. What other officers he would have to do with I do not know, but perhaps in the order of precedence at the opening of parliament and at state dinners he would pass in after the deputy minister, but I do not think that

would seriously interfere with the efficiency of the administration of the Pensions Act, or that any of the sixty or seventy odd thousand pensioners would find that they had been seriously affected by any such calamity.
Give him a title.

My hon. friend from Melfort suggests that we might give him some other title in exchange for that of deputy head.
Coming to the other portion of the amendment with regard to salaries, and so forth, it reads-I am sorry I cannot read my hon. friend's writing, so I will take the section in the old act as printed. It reads:
The salaries or other remuneration of the officers, clerks and employees of the commission, and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of this act, shall be paid out of moneys to be provided by parliament.
The bill which we have before us says with reference to salaries:
The salaries of its officers, clerks, and other employees shall be met out of the moneys provided by parliament for the purposes of the department.
With all the goodwill in the world I cannot see what difference it makes to the taxpayer whether the money is voted by parliament to the department or is voted by parliament to the board1 of pension commissioners. The power of appointment of officers is not changed. The power of selection of those who are to fill these positions remains the same as it was before. If my hon. friend would point out what change-

Perhaps if the hon. gentleman would look at the provisions of the Civil Service Act, he would see exactly what being deputy head of a department means. It is scattered all through the act. It is through the deputy head-the Board of Railway Commissioners, for instance-that the Civil Service Act functions in regard' to organization, appointments, salaries and that sort of thing.

I will come to that in a
moment, but does it make any difference to whom these salaries are voted, whether they are voted to the department, and afterwards paid out by the department to the board, or voted direct to the board? It would seem to me that it is only the difference of who shall sign the cheques, the board of pension commissioners or the departmental accountant, and possibly at the present time the same man signs the cheques anyway.

Pension Act-Mr. Power

In the one case you have
an independent commission with its own budget, so to speak, coming through. It is true that it comes through the estimates of the department, but in the other case the commission has nothing whatever to do with it; they are all officials of the department. That is the only difference.

If that is so, in one case these estimates come to the minister and are brought down to parliament under the heading: Department of Soldier's Civil Re-establishment, so many thousand dollars for the board of pension commissioners. In the other case-that which my hon. friend proposes- in the estimates we would have, still under the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; board of pension commissioners, so much-exactly the same amount. But will my hon. friend look at it from this point of view? He knows as well as I do that when an estimate is brought down from the board of pension comimssioners as such, if there has been no change the minister will simply say: This is an estimate of the board of pension commissioners:	they are an independent
body; I have nothing to do with them; you may just take the estimate or leave it, as you please, I have no control whatsoever over it. In many cases I have heard in this house and outside serious criticism of the board of pension commissioners, of its expenditure and its personnel. Up to the present the minister has been able to say: Why, I am not responsible for this; this is an absolutely independent commission. I am inclined to think that if the minister had gone a little further and taken this commission more under his control, perhaps parliament would have been better satisfied. I remember in the closing days' of last session my hon. friends opposite were imploring the minister to do something with the board, to tell the commissioners that they must see to it that their hearts were softened, that they treated the pensioners more generously. One heard from a number of hon. gentlemen accusations against members of the board to the effect that they, being independent of parliament and of the members thereof, would not give proper consideration to cases submitted to them by hon. gentlemen. The general tone of the discussion was such as to lead one to believe that the government should assume greater control in order to be able to give instructions to the board of pension commissioners. Personally I have always opposed that view. I think the board should be an independent body. It was created by the will
of parliament to be independent, so far as any body can be, of the control of politics or of the minister of the department. I think the policy then laid down was a good policy. But last session my hon. friends' opposite did not seem to agree with that view. There were exhortations from them that so and so, members of the board, had not behaved as they should, that their power should be curtailed, that they should be told they must be more sympathetic in their treatment of pensioners and of applicants. I am somewhat surprised to-day to find the same hon. members asking that the s'oeial position of the board should be made higher, if not their powers enlarged.
With regard to the suggestion by my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Geary) that this has something to do with the Civil Service Act, I am not in a position to discuss in any way, shape or form the workings of that act. I have always been opposed to it as the most iniquitous legislation that was ever enacted, and have always regarded the Civil Service Commission as the stupidest body that has ever inflicted itself on the people of Canada-
Order.

-and I am not prepared to discuss how they might or might not act or who they should or should not consult. But if they do not carry out their duties better with reference to the board of pension commissioners than they do with respect to other departments, I shall be more and more confirmed in my opinion that they should have been abolished before they were created! Whether or not any advantage will be gained by the pensioner through this body consulting with Colonel Thompson or with Dr. Amyot with regard to appointments or promotions, I am unable to say; but it seems to me that if the Civil Service Commission do consult with reference to anybody in the employ of the board of pension commissioners, they would naturally consult the head of the board. The rating would be given by the senior officers of the board.
Does not the Civil Service Act provide otherwise with regard to consultation?

It might very well provide anything. At the time I quit studying the law, I thought it such an iniquity that I did not want to be led into occasions of sin. The language which I would use with reference to it would be somewhat too expressive.

Pension Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)

Might I put my question in another form? In the opinion of the hon. gentleman, is not the commission more independent under the sections proposed to be repealed than it will be under the new enactment?

I really cannot see how the commission would be more independent under section 5 of the old act than it would be under the present legislation. This bill provides :
The commission shall be attached to the department-
Section 6 of chapter 157 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, provides:
The commission shall be attached to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment-
So far there is no change. Then this bill continues:
-and the expenses required to be incurred for the discharge of its duties, including the salaries of its officers, clerks, and other employees shall be met out of the moneys provided by parliament for the purposes of the department.
The former act provided:

and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of this act shall be paid out of moneys to be provided by parliament.
That is the situation as it existed, and I think it will remain the same after the passage of this bill as it was before. It is suggested to me by a person far more qualified to judge than I would be that the commission possibly will be more independent. I will leave it to the hon. gentleman who makes the suggestion to explain it to the house. I am free to admit that I cannot see it yet. I am willing to acknowledge that the change will not have any effect whatsoever, and for that reason I do not know why the change is included in the sugestions made by the minister.

Might I ask the hon. gentleman: Do not the proposed amendments make the commission subject to the deputy of the department, whereas in the other case under the statute as it stands the commission is subject to the minister? Under the amendments proposed is not the deputy of the department intervening to take control of the commission in a way which he cannot do now?

The board of pension commissioners is attached to the department in the same way now as before. If the commission is to be under control of the deputy minister now, without having at my disposal the statute creating the Department of Soldiers Civil Re-establishment and defining the powers of the deputy minister, I should be under the impression that the same control would exist

if the deputy minister had no control over the different branches of his department. I presume the same control would exist from the moment the commission was attached to the department as will exist under this present legislation.

I merely am trying to get
my own mind clear. The old section 5 which it is proposed to repeal provides that the commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil Service Act. Does not that section give a different status to the head of the commission, giving him the right of consultation and direction and control in respect of appointees, which he would not have if that control were placed under the deputy head of the department?

I am sorry, but I do not
[DOT]think that is the case. It may be, but I cannot see it that way. It seems to me that the powers of the chairman of the board of pension commissioners will be just as great after this act is passed as they were before. Really, I do not know why there was any change in the act unless it was to make it read better, perhaps, with reference to the social position of one or other of the heads. There was a certain amount of departmental jealously which existed and which perhaps will be wiped out now that the social standing of the respective officers has been established. I will admit that there has been perhaps a diminution in the social standing of the chairman of the board; that is as far as I am prepared to go.

I feel somewhat at a loss to follow the facetious remarks of the hon. member (Mr. Power) who has just taken his seat. It is evident that he looks upon the whole discussion as being somewhat irrelevant and humorous. However, he did commit himself to one statement which is worth the consideration of the house, and that is, to the effect that he did not know why this change should be made. But the minister in charge of the matter stated a little while ago that if the change were made nothing would be altered so far as the administration of the board of pension commissioners or of the department was concerned. In the face of both these statements alone there would seem to be very good reason for not making the change. But if we want a further -reason than that I will go back again to the point raised with respect to the powers and rights of deputy ministers, and if the hon. gentleman had taken notice of the act so much despised he would have found, first of all, that all organization of the department, all difficulty with respect to personnel of the staff,

Pension Act-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
everything affecting salary increases or decreases, classifications and revisions, are all dealt with directly by the deputy minister with the Civil Service Commission. In the Civil Service Act I find, under the classification of deputy or deputy minister, a provision to which I direct the attention of the house in view of the statement made by the minister that the railway commissioners were not and had not been regarded as deputy heads. That is what the minister stated. He nods his head; he acquiesces. Now I will quote from the Civil Service Act:
(c) "Deputy" or "deputy head" means and includes the deputy of the minister of the crown presiding over the department, the clerk of the Privy Council, the clerks of the Senate and House of Commons, the librarians of parliament, the comptroller of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Superintendent of Insurance, the Dominion Archivist, the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada and, in all cases in which such meaning is not inconsistent with his powers and duties, under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, the Auditor General.
Therefore, so far as the Civil Service Act is concerned, a railway commissioner has the right of a deputy head.
I understood that they had not that power under the act, but they have.

The minister makes an honourable amende. And now that his attitude with respect to the matter is correct, let me ask him to reconsider the position taken by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) with respect to the suggested deletion of section 5 of the old act, which reads:
5. The commission shall have all the powers and duties of a deputy head of a department for the purpose of the Civil Service Act.
2. The salaries or other remuneration of the officers, clerks and employees of the commission, and all the expenses of the commission incidental to the carrying out of this act, shall he paid out of moneys to be provided by parliament.
That classification is deleted and the board of pension commissioners are now deprived of their rank of deputy. They are deprived of direct access to the minister himself, unless by agreement or courtesy, and deprived of direct access to the Civil Service Commission unless, again, by act of courtesy. The whole thing must now be handed directly through the deputy head of the department and not because of any right vested in the board of pension commissioners itself. You have undoubtedly taken largely from the powers of the old board and rendered it completely subject to a department which is now under patronage, a department which does not come within the Civil Service Act.
To sum up the objections to the change. It may be said that the board of pension commissioners will now be definitely attached to the department itself; it will have lost its power of direct approach to the minister unless by courtesy; it will have lost its power of direct approach to the Civil Service Commission unless, again, by courtesy; the appropriations voted by parliament under the old act will now be transferred to the department, thereby transferring the staff of the board of pension commissioners, at present under the board's control, to the pay-roll of the department. Again, the board will have no staff of its own but will be entirely in the hands of the department as to what staff shall be loaned to the board of pension commissioners for the purposes of carrying out the duties of the board. The board's annual report, which heretofore was an independent document and was presented to parliament as such, will no longer be an independent document unless by agreement with the minister, but will be embodied in the annual report of the department, and will form a part of that department's report. But the principal objection I have to the whole change is, in the first place; that the direct contact of the board of pension commissioners itself, both with the minister and with the Civil Service Commission, is abolished; and in the second place the element of merit which did enter into the personnel of the board of pension commissioners is now eliminated, so that the personnel will be placed directly within and under a department which, according to my information, is not under the jurisdiction of the Civil Service Commission. I am opposed to the change, and unless the minister or someone else is in a position to correct the impressions I have formed in this matter, and which I have submitted to the house, I am afraid I shall have to suport the amendment that has been proposed.

The question is on the
amendment.
Amendment (Mr. Geary) negatived on division.
Motion agreed to, and bill read the third time and passed.

Public works-harbours and rivers, Prince Edward Island-West Point-wharf repairs, $4,000.

When these items were being considered the other evening I was directing the attention of the minister to the condition which existed in Kings county, Prince Edward Island, in relation to these estimates, and I was pointing out that with .the exception of the amounts recommended by the Duncan commission for warehouses for potato storage, last year $107,000 was voted for harbours and rivers in Prince Edward Island, of which sum only $1,000 was earmarked for Kings county, which does not seem a fair division considering the fact that there are many works in that county which require attention. For instance, at my home town of Cardigan there is a government wharf the central portion of which to the extent of 200 feet has dropped; no repairs have been made, and the structure is in an unsatisfactory state. This is a disgraceful monument to the present government. In other places there are needs equally great; Bay Fortune needs breakwater repairs; Naufrage harbour requires some expenditures to be made; Little Sands breakwater requires repairs, and there are various other places which might be named.

This year we find almost the same condition with regard to these estimates; we find a total vote of $229,000, and after you deduct $140,000 for wharf improvements and warehouses at Charlottetown you have only $89,000 left for three counties, of which the county of Kings receives only about $13,000. I consider that to be an unfair division of the amounts voted. Then we have the condition which exists at Souris East; $36,500 was voted for the breakwater there in 1925, when the constituency was represented by a Liberal. In 1926, when the county ceased to support the Liberal government and sent a representative to Ottawa who was a member of the opposition, that item of $36,500 was deleted from the estimates and has not been replaced. The need there is very great; the breakwater is in serious danger of 'breaking away and needs strengthening. A contract was let in 1925, but because of the illness of the subcontractor it was not carried out. The other evening I asked the minister for an explanation with regard to this vote for Souris East, and he gave me a suppositious answer of his own which did not meet the case at all. Now I would like the minister to tell the house why this vote was taken from the estimates. Recently we had a discussion with regard to an item for the Mahone Bay post office; that was a somewhat similar case, with the exception that the member who was able to have the Mahone Bay item struck out was lucky enough to secure another seat in the house and was therefore able to explain why the vote was struck out, and to take the responsibility for advising the minister to remove the amount from the estimates. This candidate was not lucky enough to secure another seat, and he is not here to make any admissions of that kind. The minister knows the facts, and I ask for some reasonable explanation. I do not want to leave the impression that discrimination is practised against the county because of the fact that it failed to elect a supporter of the government, but it will take an explanation on the part of the minister to avoid carrying away that idea.

Mr. Chairman,
as the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) has referred to the vote that has been given to the other county, in looking over the estimates I think I have just as much reason to complain this year as he has. The harbour improvements that were put through last year for Summerside were greatly appreciated by the people there. I think it is only fair to the Minister of Public Works that I be permitted to read a letter from R. T. Holman Limited. They are a large firm there who handle the business of the port in connection with outward and inward freight. When a little vote is made for some improvements down in the maritime provinces, the cry is raised in different quarters of the Dominion that it has been made for political reasons. They say that it is just a gratuity that is being given to keep us in line, and suggestions of that kind are always brought forward from some section of the house. I think I should be permitted to read this letter to show how the people there appreciate the work that was done last year. This letter is dated May 2, 1928, and is
addressed to myself. In part, it reads as follows:
We thought possibly you might be interested in knowing just how the sheds and storages on railway wharf have turned out, how that we have had a trial with our first fertilizer steamer.
Everyone appears to be delighted with the layout, and there is not the slightest doubt but that cargoes can be discharged at a very much lower rate than heretofore.
I am confident that there is no place on the island that can now compete with us for economy in unloading. They have been running almost steadily at a cost of less than 50 cents per ton-of course, as they come near the end of the cargo it will be more expensive-but at present indications it leads us to suppose that the cost will not be over 60 cents per ton. When we were operating with the old pier it cost us well over 90 cents, so you will see that the expenditure that you were successful in getting for your county last year is actually money saved.
We are very glad to say that, due to these facilities and the cheapness of unloading, we now have a territory to supply extending from Tignish to Hunter River. Heretofore, this territory only extended from Tignish to Emerald. The farmers beyond Emerald are large consumers of fertilizer, hence it is a very fine thing for this port.
We believe the same thing will apply in the loading of potatoes. One of the representatives of the Potato Growers' Association assured us that this would be so. The whole layout is working just as we anticipated. The farmers are getting their supplies from the western warehouses promptly and without any holdup whatever, and they do not interfere in the slightest degree with the unloading of the ship. They have been loading cars at the rate of 40 per day on the railway, and this is an exceptionally good record.
This letter follows along the same lines, and shows the benefit that this construction work has been to the people of that community, and how it is appreciated by them.
I wish again to express the thanks of the people in that vicinity and from that constituency to the Minister of Public Works for the wharf that he gave us last year, and I hope that when the supplementary estimates are brought down this county will not be forgotten.

ernment assumes the full responsibility for seeing that the Duncan report is carried out and if anything happens to that breakwater before it is improved, that will be the responsibility of the government.

Apparently
I can get no answer from the minister to the question I have been asking. He will not give me a reason. What he states as a reason is no reason whatever, and he knows it. He knows further that in the main estimates of last year the vote for the Georgetown warehouse was not in at all, and $1,000 was voted for Kings county. Let me vary my question. Does the minister propose to do anything for Souris breakwater this year in the supplementary estimates?

I would like to point out to the minister what I fancy he no doubt knows, that this is an important work. The government considered it important enough to include $36,000 in the estimates for it two years ago, but the work has not been gone on with. The minister tells parliament that if the work goes to destruction, that is a matter entirely for the government. He -would lead the house to believe that he and his department will be the only losers if the work goes to destruction, that the country is not going to suffer anything, that the only sufferer will be the government or the reputation of the government. I would remind the minister that that is not quite the position of affairs. If $36,000 -were needed for this work two years ago, the situation has not improved in the interval. The work is an important one. Is it to be allowed to go to utter destruction, or are we to wait and then expend $50,000 on it next year because the government is not expending a proper amount on it to-day? That is the situation, and some more satisfactory answer is due than we have yet received from the minister.
I want to satisfy my hon. friends, and I assure them that I want to do justice to Prince Edward Island.
Restore the vote then.

But if my hon. friends
think that I can give them a promise now that this work will be provided for in the supplementary estimates, I cannot do it, and I hope my hon. friends are sufficiently interested in that section of the country not to pursue the matter to the extent of making it more difficult for the department to do what is its duty to that riding. I have assured my hon. friends that it is the intention of the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
department to endeavour as far as it possibly can to hand out justice to the various parts of the province of Prince Edward Island, including the county of Kings. I cannot go any further than that.

The minister is not
giving me very much evidence of that intention just now. There is no doubt that everybody in connection with the Public Works department who has any knowledge of the situation at Souris knows that the breakwater is going to destruction. The government were so convinced of it themselves two years ago that they put an item of $36,000 in the estimates, and awarded a contract for the work. That work was not proceeded with, and the explanation given by the minister does not explain the matter at all. If the contract was awarded I presume the contractors came under certain obligations, and that some persons guaranteed their fulfiment. If the contractor failed' to carry it out, why did not the minister insist on the bondsmen completing the work? If this work was necessary two years ago-and it was-it is certainly more necessary to-day. It will not do for the minister to tell us on this side of the house that he is the man who is taking the loss. He is not. The country is bearing the loss, and he is responsible for that loss.

Mr. Chairman, in order not to take up the time of the house with this item, I think we may assume from the minister's last statement that he is at least giving the matter full consideration, and will have an amount in the supplementary estimates for the purpose of restoring the wharf and breakwater.
Item agreed to.

Escuminac-breakwater extensions, $52,000.
How much has been expended?

$393 under fhe present
contract.

I have not any information except with regard to the expenditures for the work that is at present going on. An order in council was passed on March 2, 1928, accepting the tender of Ashley A. Colter of Fredericton, for the construction of a breakwater extension at Escuminac, at the unit prices quoted therein, entailing an expenditure of about $61,729. What is the extent and. the nature of the traffic?
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

The engineer reports:
The work is required for the protection of the many boats fishing off this exposed coast, and for landing supplies and shipments of fish and farm produce, the locality being 32 miles from the nearest railway station.
Forty to fifty boats fish for salmon with drift nets oil Escuminac, the annual value of their catch being about $90,000, and some /0 boats fish lobsters and herring, of which the catch is valued at about $110,000. Green Point-breakwater, $44,000.

' Mr. ELLIOTT:	It is similar in some
respects to the beautiful city of which my hon. friend is a representative. It is not as completely covered with harbour works, but there is an attempt to follow that example.
There must be wharves or breakwaters to accommodate every little village and town and almost every individual.
What is the county, and the expenditure?

Is the contract let? If so,
who is the contractor?
