Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally-repairs and improvements, $45,000.
What are the items making up this $45,000?

The only information I
can give is to state what amounts have been expended in previous years. Last year the total was $36,882; 1926, $23,351; 1925, $25,577; 1924, $34,049.

Item agreed to.

Leonardville-wharf repairs, $7,000.
What county is that?

As this is the only item under which I can discuss the county of Charlotte I wish to direct the attention of the minister to a few appropriations which, in my opinion, should be made in the interests of people who, in one portion of my county, have been very loyal to this government. May I say that not one dollar appears for an}' new public works in aid of the fishing industry in Charlotte county, which is one of the best fishing areas on the Atlantic coast. There is no question about the need for this amount which is here provided for wharf repairs; it is absolutely necessary. No doubt it is needed to maintain the wharves in proper shape. But I would remind the government that during the seven years they have been in power not one dollar has been appropriated for any new public works in Charlotte county, with a single exception. That was in the year 1924 when the government themselves decided that, in the interests of the fishing industry in that part of the country, there should be a breakwater at Harrington cove. After looking over other propositions in the island they came to the conclusion that it was most important that a breakwater should be constructed at Harrington cove in the island of Grand! Manan. Engineers were sent down for the purpose and plans and specifications were made and submitted to the department. The department approved the plans and an appropriation was included in the estimates for 1925. The people were led to believe that their wants in this regard *would be satisfied at once. But for reasons best known to the government the location of that breakwater was changed overnight to Ingalls Head on the island of Grand Manan. The only reason which the people there could conceive for the change was the fact that a provincial election was about to take place in that year, 1925, and there were some rumours of discord within the ranks of the Liberal party. That was the only fact which they could think of that would influence the government in deciding upon the change. I would remind the government that in 1921, and again in 1925, the county was invaded by workers of the Liberal party, who *went to Grand Manan, Campobello and Deer island, which is a part of the county of Charlotte and which extends over a considerable coastline, and promised on every occasion that the needs of the people of these islands would be considered so far as breakwaters and wharves are concerned. There are few
*

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
breakwaters along that coastline, and these Liberal party workers promised the people there that everything necessary would be done to assist them in the industry in which they were engaged. These workers took occasion at that time to inform the people that they had been neglected from 1911 to 1921, although I wish to say to the government today that there were then in the Dominion of Canada no people more loyal to the Liberal party. They expected nothing, asked nothing and received nothing during the war period. As I say, the workers of the Liberal party went down there in 1921 and told those people that they had been neglected by the Union government which, they declared, was neither more or less than a Conservative government. And they promised the people definitely that if the Liberal party were returned to power certain public works would1 be started on Grand Manan. I repeat, these people were loyal to the Liberal party, as they always have been. I plead therefore in this house on their behalf, and I urge my hon. friends opposite to do something for them; the party are under an obligation to these people to fulfil some of the promises made them during the election of 1921 and again in 1925. I also urge that something be done, on the ground that these people are entitled to necessary works to enable them to carry on their enterprise.
In years gone by the island of Grand Manan and Deer island were prosperous fishing centres; there were thriving fishing villages on the coastline. To-day, however, they are in many cases in a dilapidated condition by reason of the fact that the younger men have left the island and gone to the United States where they can carry on their industry under more favourable conditions. If the government intend to enable these people to carry on their industry, then they are entitled to some consideration. I say, they are entitled to consideration because the industry needs it; but they are also entitled to consideration because of the promises made to the people on behalf of the government. Those promises should be fulfilled, and1 I trust that the minister will pay some attention to these representations. Let him find out for himself what the conditions are in that part of the country.
A breakwater was to be constructed at Harrington's cove but, as I say, the location was changed to Ingalls Head. It was also understood that a breakwater addition was to be made at Woodward cove, and there was to be a breakwater at Castalia, where there was a magnificent foundation for such a structure. Moreover, this is one of the
plaoes where it was definitely promised the people that a breakwater would be constructed. There was also to be an addition to the breakwater at N orth Head. These undertakings are all on file in the Department of Public Works. The engineers were sent down there previous to the elections to which I have referred, and they made certain recommendations. Their findings are on file and these works should be carried out in the interests of the people. I therefore strongly urge the government to give them proper consideration.
While I am on this subject I desire to call the attention of the minister to the fact that White Head, which is a part of the island of Grand Manan, is separated from the island and lies out in the Atlantic. There is a wharf there but the conditions are such that the fishermen can enter the harbour only at high tide. The people of the island desire that a little dredging be done there so that the fishermen may have ample opportunity to moor their boats and, in the event of a storm, to be protected from the winds and weather of the Bay of Fundy and of the Atlantic. I sincerely hope the minister will consider this point. Dredging at that wharf would cost little money and, as I say, it would afford the fishermen an ample opportunity to make a safe mooring. The same remark applies to Deer island, where a day or two of dredging would give splendid accommodation. At present in the event of storms the fishermen are obliged to moor their boats two miles from home, and this makes it very hard for the fishermen. At Stewart Town, at the upper end of Deer island, a wharf or a breakwater was promised years ago, but the people have never been given it. Necessarily, therefore, they are anxious that something shall be done. On behalf of the people of the island, who gave their generous support to the government, I plead that their claims be recognized and that steps be taken to improve the conditions under which the fishing industry is carried on.

Item agreed to.
Point Sapin-breakwater extension, $11,000.
Mr. JONES; Where is this point-in what county?

My hon. friend is not as
well up in his geography in regard to this item as he is in regard to the last three. He did not have to ask any question at all about them. This is in Kent.
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

The minister says that I am not as well up in my geography in regard to this place as I am so far as the last three are concerned. May I point out that, as regards those three, one was in Charlotte and the other in St. John, Vhose representatives are here. It seems that about the only expenditures are in the Postmaster General's county and in Northumberland. I do not think the Postmaster General has been very generous to the rest of his colleagues in the province; some of them have no expenditures at all. As regards the constituency of Royal, comprising the districts of Kings and Queens, there are more wharves in that constituency than in any other in the province and there are only two small amounts included in the whole estimate for New Brunswick, apart from the expenditure to which I have referred. Those items amount to $3,700. It looks like discrimination to me.

Item agreed to.
St. Simon-wharf, $26,000.
In what constituency is St. Simon?

It is in Gloucester county. Item agreed to.
Traeadie harbour-breastworks and breakwaters, $20,000.
What county is this in? I would like to have some explanation as to these expenditures, as to whether or not this contract has been let and what amount has been expended?
Traeadie harbour is in Gloucester county and this amount of $20,000 is a revote as my hon. friend will see if he looks at the estimates. It is to complete work already under contract.
How much has been expended?
Only $124.
Last year?
Yes, last year.

Item agreed to.
Quebec-Beaupre-dredging-Ste. Anne Paper Company to contribute one-third of cost, $122,-
000.
In what county is this?
This is a rather large vote, and I would ask the minister to explain it.

It is required to provide for the department's share of the balance necessary to complete the dredging contract
[Mr. Elliott. 1
with the Canadian Dredging Company Limited, which contract has been already let. The contract is for dredging a 14-foot channel 4,060 feet long by ISO feet wide at the upper end and tapering to 200 feet wide at the outer end with a turning basin 14 feet deep at the site of the new wharf of the St. Anne Paper Company.
What is the total amount of the contract?
The contract is for $218,420.
Is it the policy of the government to do work of this kind for private companies?

Where a company is carrying on a business which promises to be extensive, and where they build wharves and make an expenditure of a million dollars it is the policy of the government to do dredging in order to provide access to those wharves.
It depends a good deal upon which province the expenditure is made in.
I think that is the policy in all the provinces, as my hon. friend will find if he follows the estimates through.
Does the expenditure have to be a million dollars or over by the private company before the government will help?

I do not recall that we have aided any company where the expenditure was under a million dollars, but if it were a concern which promised to create wealth and develop business in that particular community, personally I would feel like looking very carefully into the matter to see what could be done to encourage such development.
Is this work done specifically for a private company or is this a public waterway?
My hon. friend will understand that this is on the St. Lawrence.
Did the company build the wharves at their own expense?
Yes.
Then what would be the position of any other person who desired to use these wharves?

We have an agreement with the company by which they allow the public to use the wharves.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
Will the public be re quired to pay any charges?
No.

Item agreed to.
Cap Chat-wharf extension and repairs, $30,-
000.
Will the minister explain this item?

This amount of $30,000 is required to complete the contract for the construction of an extension to this wharf 500 feet in length by a width of 25 feet at the top and having an average height of 20 feet, to be built in close faced square timber ballasted with stone, covered with a 3-inch flooring and provided with fenders spaced 8 feet apart; and to carry out minor repairs to the approach.
Was this contract let by tender?
Yes.
What will be the total length of the wharf when it is completed?
This extension is 500 feet in length, and I am advised that the total length will be probably 1,000 feet.
What is the nature of the business carried on there?
Export pulpwood. I think my hon. friend asked if this contract had been let by tender. It was; this was the lowest of eight tenders received after advertisements had been issued.
With regard to these items of $1,000, $5,000 and so on scattered throughout the estimates, would the minister say whether that work is carried on under contract or whether it is done by day labour?
The work under the small votes is usually done by day labour.
Under the control of the department?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Cap de la Madeleine-wharf extension and repairs, $58,500.
Will the minister explain this item?

This amount is required to complete a contract for the construction of a cribwork extension to the downstream end of headblock 200 feet long by 90 feet wide. This is necessary to provide for the constantly increasing traffic. The present wharfage is entirely inadequate for the growing population, which has increased from 2,101 in 1911 to 6,738 under the 1921 census.
Is the business increasing in proportion to the increase in population?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Cap Rouge-wharf and dredging-the St. Regis Paper Company of Canada to contribute one-third of cost, $30,000.
I see this is another paper company. Will the minister explain this item?

This is a revote; this amount was voted last year. The company had not advanced sufficiently for the department to feel justified in letting the contract, so no contract was let, but it is expected it will be. This wharf and dredging is required in connection with the large pulp and paper mill to be commenced here by the St. Regis Paper Company in 1928, which will employ about 2,000 men, and is expected to increase the population of Cap Rouge from 500 to over 10,000, and contribute a large revenue to the Canadian National Railways.
What is the estimated cost?
In the vicinity of $277,000.
Will this amount complete it?
It is just beginning it.

Is this not purely a provincial rather than a national matter? It seems to me that if a paper company in one of the western provinces needed a waterway they would have to provide it, or the province itself would have to do it.

That is not the case in Manitoba. I have in mind a lumber company at Black island in lake Winnipeg which built a wharf of their own. The government has done the dredging to that wharf, and that makes an extra harbour on the lake which is very valuable to the fishermen and to those carrying on shipping there. They have this additional harbour of refuge in case of need, and in that way it is a public service.

Item agreed to.
Crabtree Mills-reconstruction of ice breaker, $2,500.
What does that refer to?

This is a balance due,
under contract, for the reconstruction of a
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

cribwork and concrete icebreaker in the Quareau river near the village of Crabtree Mills. This icebreaker was damaged in the spring of 1927.

Item agreed to.
Doucet's landing (Ste. Angele de Laval) - wharf reconstruction, $93,000.
Is that where the late member landed with the Margaret?

This work is under contract, and the amount is needed to complete the reconstruction and enlargement of the headblock of the Canadian National railway wharf. It is under contract with Messrs. Farley & Grant.
Do the Canadian National Railways own that wharf?
It has been turned over to the government, who now own it. It was formerly a railway wharf.
How many railway wharves has the department taken, over?

Four have been taken
over, and three are yet under consideration.
Is that a new policy?
No.

I am just wondering how
that works out. When we consider the railway estimates the Canadian National Railways would normally have this expenditure.

These were wharves that were owned' by the Intercolonial railway. Negotiations have been pending for some time between the two departments for the taking over of these wharves, and in this and three other cases they have been completed. It was thought it was in the public interest to do this.
Has the department asked that these wharves be taken over?
Not this department.
Did the Railway department approach your department to take them over?

On the request of the
Railway department.

I suppose the railway
uses them now.
Oh, yes, they are public wharves.
They were not getting rid of a very good wharf.
It is not usually the best wharves that they are most anxious to get rid of.

Mr. Chairman, will the
minister be good enough to tell us the policy of the government in regard to these wharves? I have asked for this information on several occasions. First, I had a denial that they were taking over the wharves; then there was an admission that they were taking over one wharf, and then another one. In the present case we have one in the province of Quebec.
Where there is a wharf that will serve the public for general purposes, the policy of the department is to take it over.

For fifty and indeed for sixty _ years the policy was that the Intercolonial railway bulilt, maintained, repaired and controlled its own wharves. Will the minister be good enough to tell us the reason for the departure from that procedure?

The argument was that if we were furnishing wharves for the use of the public generally there was no reason why they should not be maintained by the government, and serve the purpose of the railway as well.

That is hardly answering the question. Railway wharves are railway wharves; they are not public wharves. There are very few railway wharves that could be termed public wharves, in any sense of the term. That point was raised in connection with the wharves at Pictou. They are not public wharves, they are absolutely and entirely railway wharves, always were, and always will be. The real effect of this will be that the Railway department will be relieved of the cost of maintaining and repairing these wharves, and the Public Works department, or the country as a whole, is going to take over a burden that was formerly borne by the railway. I am sorry that the Minister of Railways is not here, his department is to be relieved of that amount, and his accounts will consequently make a better showing than they otherwise would. If this is the correct thing to do in connection with this department, there are other departments that might be relieved as well.
I think I am correct in saying that all the wharves in this category were formerly wharves of the government railway, and our instructions are that they are now being used for general purposes.

No, no.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
And are being taken over for that reason.

That story will not wash at all. I have said already, and I repeat, that the wharves to which I have referred are railway wharves pure and simple, not public wharves. Any statement to the contrary is not correct, and I think the minister should admit that. The question of their being public wharves falls to the ground^ The point is that you are relieving the railway of a certain amount of work and expense formerly borne by the Intercolonial, indeed from the inception of the road fifty-eight or sixty years ago down to the present time. Why has there been a change of policy?
I do not know that I can say to my hon. friend that there is any change of policy. That I think has been the policy decided upon for some time past.
No, only this year.

Whether or not they were formerly used entirely by the railway, they will in the future be public wharves and be capable of being used for any purpose for which the public may require to use a wharf. There is no doubt about what my hon. friend says. The railway department is being relieved of a certain liability which it had before, but we are getting the wharf.

In view of the fact that the railway is being relieved of the upkeep of its property which is absolutely necessary for conducting its business, has the minister made any arrangement with the Minister of Railway for a reduction in freight rates? If not, I think this is something that should be considered.
There is no special arrangement in connection with these particular wharves. My hon. friend is aware of certain reductions that have been made in freight rates.

That has nothing
to do with this.
No, but of course it takes revenue from the railway and perhaps is one reason why it is entitled to some consideration.

Is the effect of this
policy not likely to be that the deficit which we have on the eastern section of the Canadian National Railways will be much reduced by what the department has taken over in connection with these particular works, and will it not therefore be possible to reduce the rates?

This will affect the rates
very slightly, we think.

Let us have the
benefit of whatever reduction there may be, whether it be large or small. As I have said before, the upkeep of these wharves is absolutely necessary. If you cut them off, you might as well cut off a freight shed anywhere along the line. If you cut off these freight sheds, the railway cannot carry on its business. If the Public Works department is to relieve the railway of all liabilities in connection with that property, surely we are entitled to a reduction in rates comparable with the cost of the upkeep?

There is no thought of
taking over the railway wharves at Halifax.

The matter is becoming
more confused all the time. We were told not very long ago that the intention was to take over all the wharves in the Maritime provinces. The minister refers to these wharves being in the future public wharves. The mere taking of them over by his department does not make them public wharves, does not change them in any way so that the public can use them where they have not been using them before. As I have already stated, the two wharves at Pictou are simply railway wharves and they cannot be used for any other purpose. They are just as necessary foi the railway as is the track, as are the railway sidings, as are the approaches to the railway property. They are indeed: approaches to terminals of the railway property. Coastal boats come in and use them to embark freight and passengers which come over the road. These same boats land freight and passengers which in turn go over the road. All freight handled by the railway is and can be handled only over these wharves, on the freight sheds thereon and no other work is or can be done over them. The real fact, I fancy, is that the president of the road, Sir Henry Thornton, has been shrewd enough to conceive the idea of unloading these wharves on to the Public Works department and so escape the cost of upkeep and maintenance. Let the minister be frank about the matter and tell us whether or not that is true.

What has taken place is
this. Requests were made by the Department of Railways in regard to a number of wharves and a list was furnished. The contention was that they were wharves which should be taken over and maintained at government expense. The main reason that was urged for that course was that they were wharves that could be used as public wharves.

No, absolutely no.
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

There may be exceptions.
My hon. friend states something of his own knowledge and I am not in a position to contradict him. All I can say is that we are only taking over wharves which our engineers, after going over the list, said could properly be taken over as public wharves to be used by the public.

The minister has in the
estimates, and quite properly so, a sum of $25,000 to repair these railway wharves at Pietou. Those wharves should have been repaired years ago by the Railway department. They allowed them to deteriorate until they are and have been for two or three years actually dangerous to shipping and the public who use them. Now the Department of Public Works are taking them over and are relieving the railway of that amount of expense. All I want to ask of the minister is to be frank enough to say that is being done.

I have no doubt that is
correct.
Thank you.

Item agreed to.
Ellis bay harbour improvements, $300,000.

In what county is Ellis
Bay? Is it a big place?

It is in Charlevoix-
Saguenay.
What is this for?

This amount of $300,000
is required towards the completion of the contract with the Canadian Dredging Company, Limited, for dredging a channel 3,950 feet long by 300 feet wide leading to the Anticosti corporation wharves, deepening the berths at the company's commercial wharf and dredging a turning basin, all to a depth of 20 feet below low water. The Anticosti corporation has under way at the present time a scheme for the development of this harbour which involves the expenditure of approximately $2,500,000 exclusive of railroads, dwellings and buildings which it will be necessary to construct on the island. Construction work was commenced by this company on December 1, 1926, and two ship berths were ready on June 1, 1927, new commercial wharf on July 31, and harbour works completely finished by December 1, 1927.

It is a big construction
work, a large development, and the expenditure already has been large.
How much has parliament voted and how much has been expended already? I see there was a vote of $150,000 last year.

The amount expected to
complete will be $525,000.

Can the minister give us
a little fuller justification. I think he catches my point.

I caught my hon. friend's
point, and I must say that it is one that caused me a good deal of concern a year ago.

Is this on Anticosti
island?

Yes. When the company [DOT]
started on this work they interviewed the government to see whether or not the government would feel disposed to assist them, by way of dredging, in getting to their wharves. This is not a work which would have been necessary if the wharf were in the main channel of the river, but it is necessary in order that they can get from the main channel to their pulp mill. As a result of this development, 5,000 people are expected to be furnished with employment. It will be a large concern if the expectations of the company are at all fulfilled, and it is thought that in view of the revenue the government will eventually derive, it is a good business proposition.
What will the government ever get out of it?
All the shipping that takes place will enure to the benefit of the government.
How?
There will be no harbour or wharfage dues.

No.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
What, then, can the government get out of the shipping?
Everything that enters into a development of this kind increases the business of the country. We get customs revenue, for instance, and excise revenue.
For gin, or what?

I should
think that the provincial government will benefit most from the sale of timber limits, and so forth, and I would say that the expenditure should be largely undertaken by the provincial government.

I do not know whether
my hon. friend was in before when this matter was being discussed. It is not a work that the provincial government would be expected to carry on; it is not done by provincial governments, so far as I know, in any province. This is to give encouragement to an industry that is coming to the country, investing a large amount of money and engaging a large amount of labour, and expecting a large output of its products.

Who owns
Anticosti Island now?
It is the Anticosti Corporation.

Who are
the directors or the controlling influence in the Anticosti Corporation?
I could not say.

I am informed, perhaps not on reliable authority, but if I am wrong, I should like to be corrected, that this corporation is mostly composed of Americans and that the island of Anticosti belongs altogether to private individuals. Is that true?

I have no doubt that in
practically all these large companies there is a number of Americans. I think this is an amalgamation of three companies; it is a large concern, but I could not give the personnel.

I was a moment ago
drawing attention to the only possible justification for an expenditure of this kind, and unfortunately this does not apparently come within that classification. Where there is a public channel, the channel of a river, stream or bay or harbour, the government is entitled out of the public revenue to put
that channel into shape and maintain it in shape so as to serve a community. But here we have a private corporation owning, as I understand, the whole island of Anticosti- the sole owner of the island, I believerputting in a large industrial plant. We all welcome the establishment of industries; there is no question about that, but in the erection of this plant the company is building wharves, pulp mills and such like, and we are asked to spend $500,000 merely to dredge out from the navigation channel to the private wharves of the company or to the pulp mill, as the case might be. I think that work should be done by the company itself. If there is any part of the construction that is absolutely essential, it is the dredging to the company's own wharves, and certainly they ought to do that work out of their own funds. I understand that there is another item somewhat similar to this in this same vote, where we are asked to vote $100,000 for Manicouagan river. In that case the company is paying one-half of the cost of the work. Is that not so?
One-third.

Well, a portion of the
cost, one-third; and I say that this company on Anticosti Island ought to pay its share of this work. Personally, in the absence of some extraordinary circumstance, I think they ought to pay the whole cost, and certainly the minister has not yet given us any justification for an expenditure of $500,000 for the benefit of this one company. As regards possible revenue to the government, the only revenue there will be will come from the fact of people living in the country-that is all, an indirect benefit.

Income tax,
perhaps.

Let us hope there will
be; we hope the company will be successful. But there will be no such thing as harbour or wharfage dues. There is nothing coming to the public from this improvement to navigation, I assume that nothing can be done to stop the contract; it is already let, and the work is going on. All we can do is to call attention to the matter, and certainly offer our criticism of this method of procedure. There is another point. The original vote was for $150,000. I do not know whether we were informed when that $150,000 was voted, whether the total contract was to exceed $500,000.

I remember stating that
that was just a beginning.
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

I am not in a position to criticize even that statement, but the original vote was for $150,000, and now we are asked to vote $300,000, and I suppose there will be another vote next year to complete the contract.
This completes it.

Then there must have
been a further vote, because last year's vote and this only makes $450,000, and the total cost is over $500,000.
The hon. member is right, there will be $75,000.

Thera will >be another
vote next year. Well, I do not think the minister feels very comfortable about this vote. That native honesty which characterizes him is shining out of his face and he looks mighty uncomfortable in supporting this vote. I give him credit at least for a twisted conscience, if nothing else, and I do not know that we can do anything more than give it a little extra twist so that this will not occur again.

I join my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in protesting against votes of this kind. Here are extremely wealthy companies asking the government to do their work for them. Anticosti is in a peculiar situation. I could understand the advisability of giving help at Mani-couagan or Bersimis, or at some other point along the lower St. Lawrence where it might be possible that eventually settlement would be developed. These moneys would help in the development of that region. But Anticosti until a few years ago was in the possession of the Menier family of Paris, France. They were granted powers greater than we would think of granting to-day; they had almost the power of life and death over the people of the island.
Mr. LAPOINTE. But they never got one cent of money for public works.

I was coming to that. The
Anticosti Corporation took over this island from the Menier family. It is composed of three of the largest pulp and paper groups in the province of Quebec-not favourable to the government, I may say. Sir Herbert Holt, who is a director of the corporation, is on the directorate of 130 or 140 companies. There is no question of the Anticosti Corporation settling the island. They are coming to us in the guise of beggars and tell-

ing us that they want this particular port developed ,but as soon as they have cut all the pulpwood off the island the works will be abandoned, and the country will have spent that much and be out the interest simply to provide facilities for the corporation to clear off the wood. Personally I do not think there will be a settlement there fifteen years hence.

The house resumed from Wednesday, May 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. Morin (St. Hyacinthe-Rouville) for the third reading of Bill No. 43, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Garland (Bow River).

In offering a few remarks on this question I do so not in the spirit of obstructing the bill. The Bell Telephone Company, like any other company, has the right to come to parliament and ask for legislation, and the only reason I have for objecting to this measure is the fact that, in my opinion, the Bell Telephone Company have very extensive powers which are invoked to the injury and prejudice of many of the users of telephones throughout the Dominion. That fact was particularly emphasized a year ago in an application made by the company for an increase in rates. I believe they have made applications in previous years for similar increases which have not been granted. They claimed that they were not making sufficient from the existing rates and that they required extra money. Their application was opposed by a number of persons, corporations and provinces in the Dominion. I find on the record that the opponents of the application for the increased rates included the government and the Attorney General of Ontario, the city of Montreal, the city of Toronto, the city of Hamilton, the city of Ottawa, the Union of Canadian Municipalities and the city of Brantford. The application was heard in the latter part of 1926 and an order was made early in 1927. The city of which I represent a portion was largely interested in that application, the re-

Bell Telephone Company
suit of which was very unsatisfactory; and as a representative from that city I feel it my duty to voice what I believe is the prevailing sentiment of the people there.
The company has now a capitalization of $75,000,000, which represents 750,000 shares. Of that amount $63,000,000 has been issued and allotted and there is something in the neighbourhood of $12,000,000 of Stock in the treasury at par value. It has been alleged by the company, in making this application, that their reason for asking for this extension to capitalization is an immediate need of $20,000,000 for the purposes of extension and so forth in connection with the company. The $12,000,000 at par value represents simply $12,000,000-that is, 120,000 shares of stock. The Bell Telephone is probably one of the best securities in Canada; there is no difficulty in getting the public to invest in these stocks and securities. When therefore the company says that it requires $20,000,000 immediately, all it has to do is to place that
120.000	shares on the market from time to time as the money is required. If it does so it will be able to get all the money it requires for immediate needs, and that is not for use immediately nor in the next month or two, but over a considerable period.
It may be of interest to point out that the company has not at any one time put on the market 120,000 shares of stock. In 1894 they placed 9,900 shares with their shareholders; they allotted that much at par. They received into the treasury $990,000. During that year the lowest price quoted on their stock on the market was 172 and the peak price that year was 193. As I say, they placed only 9,900 shares at that time. In 1907 they placed 25,000 shares at par with their stockholders and the prices that year ran from 115 to 145. In 1911 they placed another 25,000 at par, the prices ranging from 140 to 153. I could go down the list, to the year 1925, and show that at no time during that whole period was the stock at less than par except in one year, 1921, when the range was from 99} to 112. In that year they allotted 57,250 shares to their stockholders, and in 1924 they issued -the largest number of shares in any one year'-82,272 shares, allotted to the shareholders at par. At no time have they issued or sold or allotted more stock at par value than in that year. In 1902 they allotted
10.000	at 125; in 1904, 20,000 at 125; in 1905,
10.000	at 125; in 1908, the same amount at 125; and in 1925 they allotted amongst their employees 4,250 shares at 110. The prices have ranged from 99} to 193. There has been
no difficulty whatsoever in the company selling its stock at any time.
From 1886 this company has been earning more than its dividend requirements of 8 per cent, and since 1895 it has paid continuously a dividend of 8 per cent on its capital stock issue. So the company has had no difficulty in paying the 8 per cent dividend, which as a matter of fact is secured by orders of the railway board which, in fixing rates, always has taken into consideration the necessity of meeting that 8 per cent dividend. In its application to the board last year the company stated that the reason they requested an increase in rates was because they needed the money for extensions and so on; they now come forward and ask to increase their capitalization for the very same reason. I say that if they take the 120,000 shares of stock from the treasury and offer them to the public they can get enough money for their extensions without this additional capitalization. This increase will give them a greater opportunity to hand out stock to their shareholders at par value from time to time as they may see fit, thus giving the stockholders what might be called a melon, or the difference between the par value and the market value of the stock. At present rates this would amount to the difference between $100 and about $170 per share, which would be received by the shareholders. The citizens of Toronto are very much dissatisfied with the result of the application which was made to the board last year; they are opposed to this increase in capitalization. They say, and I think they are entitled to believe, that if the Bell Telephone Company used its revenues economically there would be no need to ask for this increase in capital and there would be no justification for offering stock to their shareholders at par value.
From their revenue accounts they have extracted-and I do not use that word in an offensive manner-very large sums of money which have been used for different purposes and which are not taken into consideration in fixing the rates charged telephone users. I would like to bring to the attention of the house some ways in which this is done. A number of years ago this company established a pension fund, which amounted to $911,777 in 1926. This was built up from the revenues of the company, and did not include any contributions from company employees or officers. This fund was established for the purpose of providing insurance for the employees and officers of the Bell Telephone Company, yet they do not contribute to it.
Bell Telephone Company

In 1927 that fund amounted1 to about $1,200,000, and in order to get rid of that amount so that it would not appear in the accounts of the company the fund was incorporated and is now known as the Bell Telephone Company Benefit Fund. This money was transferred to that fund and does not appear in the accounts of the company, and each year the fund is augmented by contributions from the revenues of the company. When the company applied to the railway board last year those who were opposed to the in-cz'ease were not permitted to inquire into that fund, as to how the moneys were being used, how they were invested and the income received; that was a closed book. That meant that the users or lessees of telephones throughout Ontario and Quebec were refused information with regard to an amount which is increasing year by year, an amount made up from the revenues of the Bell Telephone Company, which revenues are obtained from the tolls and rates charged.
There is another method by which certain moneys have been taken from the revenue account, as to which the users of telephones have been refused information. About 1895, although I am not sure of the exact date, in order to manufacture articles other than telephone apparatus, supplies and equipment, which they were entitled to do under their original charter, the Bell Telephone Company caused another company to be incorporated, which was known as the Northern Electric and Manufacturing Company. Until that time the Bell Telephone Company manufactured their own supplies and equipment; they had a certain plant for that purpose and they found that the plant was capable of manufacturing other articles but could not do so because the company were not authorized to manufacture anything but telephone equipment. They applied for the incorporation of this company; the application was granted and the company incorporated with a small capitalization. In 1914 certain other amalgamations were effected; up until that year the Bell Telephone Company furnished all the money for the purposes of the Northern Electric and Manufacturing Company, which money came from the revenues of the Bell Telephone Company. In 1914 the assets of the Northern Electric and Manufacturing Company were transferred to another concern known as the Northern Electric Company, which is the present subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company. The Northern Electric Company is capitalized at $6,000,000; of that amount about $3,000,000 of stock is held by the Bell Telephone Company; 43 per cent 
of the stock, or less than $3,000,000 worth, is held by the Western Electric Company of Chicago, a concern which manufactures material for the American Telephone and Telegraph Company and which practically controls the manufacture of telephone and telegraph apparatus in the United States. The balance of the stock of the Northern Electric Company is held by the directors of the Bell Telephone Company, and just here I might say that the directors of the Bell Telephone Company are practically the same as the directors of the Northern Electric Company. So it will be seen that the Northern Electric Company is really a subsidiaiy of the Bell Telephone Company and is controlled by that concern. The Bell Telephone Company purchases all its apparatus and equipment from the Northern Electric Company, at prices which are fixed by the latter company. When the Bell Telephone Company manufactured its own apparatus, that apparatus was furnished at cost; they followed the practice adopted by Henry Ford, who manufactures everything going into the construction of his automobile, even owning iron and coal mines and operating a railway in order that the cost might be reduced to a minimum. The Bell Telephone Company were in that position; they obtained their supplies at cost in the first instance, but since 1914 they have paid whatever the Northern Electric Company charged them.
This latter company has been very successful; it pays a dividend of 8 per cent together with a bonus of 2 per cent, and that dividend and bonus are paid to the Bell Telephone Company. If it stopped at that I would say nothing about it; I would have no particular criticism to offer, but there is another interlocking which takes away from tihe Bell Telephone Company everything it receives from the Northern Electric Company, and a good deal in addition, namely, the interlocking arrangement between the American Telephone & Telegraph Company and the Bell Telephone Company, to which I will refer a little later on.
A report which was filed in 1926 shows that the Northern Electric Company had a surplus, including buildings and real estate, valued at $5,388,718. Their depreciation reserve -set aside to meet depreciation in the plant amounted to $5,564,249. Besides that, they held undivided money amounting to $2,844,821. Counsel representing the opponents in the application of 1926 endeavoured to get at these figures to discover the prices that the Bell Telephone Company were paying the Northern Electric for their materials

Bell Telephone Company
and the reason why this large amount of depreciation and undivided money was held. This was refused by the Board of Railway Commissioners. I do not know why the Board of Railway Commissioners took this stand, but I believe that they were quite unjustified in this position. When this board was established the intention was that it would be a tribunal different from our courts of law and different from the railway committee of the House of Commons, which formerly had dealt with railway matters. The object was to give to the citizens of this country a tribunal which was composed not of judges but of legal men and laymen throughout the Dominion. The commissioners were at first empowered to adjudicate upon matters which might come under the Railway Act, and afterwards their jurisdiction was extended to the act relating to telephones and telegraphs.
This board claimed that they had not the right to inquire into the financial condition of the Northern Electric Company, and they refused point blank to allow evidence of that character to be produced. The result is that a large part of the capital of the Bell Telephone Company is bound up in this Northern Electric Company, and we have no means of scrutinizing or investigating it.
The American Telephone and Telegraph Company is one of the largest organizations in the United States. It is not incorporated in Canada. It is a peculiar organization; it depends upon a great number of charters for its existence, some forty or fifty, and practically controls all the telephone and telegraph operations in the United States. This American company holds 32 per cent of the stock of the Bell Telephone Company, and practically controls that company. It may be said that 32 per cent is not a majority of the stock, but it is not necessary to have a majority of the stock of a company in order to ensure control; experts have alleged that 20 per cent is sufficient to effect that end. This would not be true if it were a small company where the stock is held by a small number of shareholders, but in a company the size of the Bell Telephone Company, the stock of which is held by many shareholders, 32 per cent in one block is a large amount, and will enable the interests holding it to control the company.
Will the hon. member be kind enough to tell us the source of his information and statistics?
The figures I am giving you were all produced at the application made in 1926, and are there for anyone to see.
The evidence given before the Board of Railway Commissioners.

The evidence and the arguments and statements were all filed.
I have further authority from a publication issued in New York by the Bell Telephone Securities Company, Incorporated, 195 Broadway, New York City. Their publication of April 1, 1925, stated that the American Telephone and Telegraph Company owns 32 per cent of the capital stock of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada. They not only control that stock, but they control the patents under which operations are carried on.
The Western Electric Company, to which I have already referred, owns 43 per cent of the stock of the Northern Electric Company. This company is practically owned by the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, which holds 98 per cent of the Western Electric stock. In other words, the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, through their control of the Western Electric Company, holds 43 per cent of the stock of the Northern Electric Company. The patents, as I have said, belong to the American Telephone and Telegraph Company.
The American Telephone and Telegraph Company, under a contract made in 1923, get l\ per cent of the gross revenue of the Bell Telephone Company. They get this percentage for no other reason than the fact that they have a strangle hold on the Bell Telephone Company. Through the Canadian company being obliged to use their patents, they get 1^ per cent of the total revenue, no matter whether they do anything to increase that revenue or not. They get a portion of the long distance revenue, but they earn that. They get their dividends on the 32 per cent of stock. They also have the right to call for 32 per cent of all new stock that may be issued by the Bell Telephone Company. It has been the practice of the Bell Telephone Company to issue their stock at par, excepting the occasions I have mentioned, and this would mean that the American company would get the stock at par. They would get the difference between the par value and the market value of the stock, simply by being stockholders to the extent of 32 per cent. In 1923 the American Telephone and Telegraph Company obtained from the Bell Telephone Company $330,000; in 1924, they obtained 1360,000; in 1925, $390,000, and in 1926, $450,000. In 1926, when the application was heard, it was estimated that if the rates were raised
Bell Telephone Company

according to the schedule filed, the amount the American company would receive for 1927 would be $510.000.
The following interesting dialogue took place at that application between one of the witnesses and one of the commissioners. The question being discussed was the l\ per cent of the gross revenues which the American Telephone and Telegraph Company received. Commissioner Lawrence says:
This is self explanatory, and might be of interest to the telephone users of Ontario and Quebec.
What is vour service contract expense in 1925 ?-$390,000.
And in 1926?-$420,000.
That is under the present rates?-Yes.
Under the rates asked for how much would they be in 1927?-$480,000.		
That is really on the basis of $32,000,000, is it not?
I worked it out, Mr. Geary, I think it must be that. On the basis of $30,000,000 it is $450,000, and on $32,000,000 it would be $480,000.
So that you note an increase to just $816,000 to get an extra $30,000. You make it $510,000. Is that right?-Yes.
That is, your revenue if you get the proposed increase in 1927 would provide the American Telephone & Telegraph Company with an increase automatically of $30,000?-Yes.
It would entitle the American Telephone & Telegraph Company to that amount of money? Yes.	.
And bring your receipts within $816,000 of the amount required to give them still another $30,000?-That is right.	.
The hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary) was counsel for the city of Toronto on that occasion. He said:
The point of my question is this: that automatically and without any further growth _ of business at all, an increase of rates would immediately jump your contract expenses up $30,000? .
That is correct. The contract speaks for itself. It says, payment on revenue.
That is without any extra service or anything of that sort?	_
Commissioner Lawrence:	Do I understand'
that that is without any extra service?
Mr. Geary: If the company was able to get the increase asked there would be $30,000 more payable to the American Telephone & Telegraph Company at once, without their having to take on any extra complexity of plant or anything like that.
Commissioner Lawrence: I think there should be an investigation of the transactions between these companies, for a contract that will automatically without any further growth in business or any extra service, immediately jump the contract expenses up $30,000 is unfair to subscribers of the Bell Telephone Company.
One would have thought that would be sufficient for the Board of Railway Commissioners to recommend to parliament or to the government that an amendment be made to the act in order that such an investigation might be carried out, but I do not know that such a recommendation has been made and

so far as I am aware no mention has been made of one. If it has not been made, the Board of Railway Commissioners are to that extent derelict in their duty to the people of Canada. The American Telephone and Telegraph Company is more or less of an octopus. It has a strangle hold not only upon the Bell Telephone Company but apparently upon the people of the United States. I noticed in the columns of a local paper, the Ottawa Journal, of yesterday morning this item:
Directors of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company cut the long expected "melon," to-day by authorizing the issuance of 185,000,000 additional stock at $100 to their 435,000 shareholders.
And in the Journal this morning in the same column I find the following:
American Telephone was in brisk demand throughout the session as a result of the preposed increase of $185,000,000 in capitalization with the issuance of valuable "rights" to shareholders, closing about 12 points higher at 2081 after having established a new high record for all time at 211.
That stock, which has a par value of 100, was selling yesterday at 208d and at one time it reached 211. The difference between 100 and 211 is the melon that is referred to, and the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, on account of their being in the strangle hold of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company, is compelled to contribute to that melon. That, I think, is a very important reason why we should know about the doings of that company, which is not a subsidiary but a company which practically owns the Bell Telephone Company.
Another method by which money is taken out of the Bell Telephone Company's revenue has to do with the question of depreciation. A depreciation reserve is quite a proper thing and I have no objection to a depreciation reserve being established. The Bell Telephone Company from 1880 to 1907 did not have any depreciation reserve; they carried on their repairs and renewals out of revenue. But about 1907, when they were about to become regulated in regard to rates by the Board of Railway Commissioners, they established a depreciation reserve, and from 1907 to 1926 they had contributed from the revenues of the company to that reserve the sum of $38,653,562. Of that amount, however, they used for the purpose of renewals and repairs only $13,770,047, leaving in that reserve account $24,883,505 unused. The evidence that was given on the application in 1926 by Mr. Lash, the chief engineer, showed that the plant and equipment of the Bell Telephone Company was 100 per cent efficient. The reason he gave for that was that the depreciation had been made up year by

Bell Telephone Company
year by prompt renewals and repairs, the total of which, as I said before, was $13,770,047. The plant is 100 per cent efficient. Another officer of the Bell Telephone Company on that investigation stated that the best experience for establishing a reserve fund was the past experience of the company. The past experience of the company showed that from 1907 to 1926 renewals and repairs amounted to only $13,770,047, and that was taken out of the depreciation reserve fund leaving the large amount of nearly $25,000,000 unexpended. It might be well for us to say to the Bell Telephone Company: Why not take that and use it for the purpose of making the extensions, renewals and repairs that you want to make at the present time? That will more than cover the $20,000,000 that you require. It is rather strange that on the application the Board of Railway Commissioners did not take into consideration the question of depreciation. It did not take into consideration either the interest of the Northern Electric Company or that of the American Telephone and Telegraph Company in the Bell Telephone Company. That is a reason why an increase of $75,000,000 in capitalization should not be authorized until some conditions or restrictions are placed upon the Bell Telephone Company in the use of its revenue.
I am heartily in accord with the amendment. I think the stock of the Bell Telephone Company should be placed on the market at a restricted price. The amendment proposes that the stock should not be sold except by public subscription. The Bell Telephone Company, as I have s'tated before, at no time except on the occasions in 1902, 1904, 1905, 1906 and 1925 sold or allotted their stock at anything more than par. In 1925 they sold a small block at 110 to their employees and in 1902, 1904, 1905 and 1906 they sold stock at 125 to their shareholders. I say that they should be forced at the present time to go into the market and sell their stock at a fair price. If they were not looking to the people of Canada for their revenue in the way they do in the shape of tolls, I would say that we might be interfering with their financing. But in case of a stringency or deficiency of funds they come back and say that they want their rates raised in order to make up that deficiency. In this case they are asking for an increase in capitalization, and I want to cite two. or three companies that do not allow their stock to be allotted to their shareholders at par, but that insist upon its being sold to them at a premium. The stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company is a par value of $100 and yet I find in their 56103-199
report for the year ended December 31, 1927, on page 7, this statement under the heading of "Issue of Additional Common Stock":
Pursuant to the authorization given at the last annual meeting, the directors of the company decided to issue 400,000 shares of additional ordinary capital stock, of which 325,000 shares were offered for subscription by shareholders at the price of $150 per share.
In other words, 50 per cent more than the par value of that stock went into the treasury of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and not into the pockets of the shareholders. The report continues:
And 50,000 shares were offered for subscription by the officers and employees of the company at the same price. As the applications for stock by officers and employees exceeded by 6,290 shares the amount offered, your directors decided to increase the number of shares available for this purpose to 56,290 shares.
Had the 325,000 shares been sold at par, they would have realized $32,500,000; actually they realized $48,350,000. The 6,290 shares if sold at par would have'brought in $6,290,000; actually they brought in $9,435,000. There were still left unsold of that issue 18,710 shares, in regard to which the directors say:
The remaining 18.710 shares will be disposed of in the market when conditions warrant such disposal.
And the market for that stock to-day, Mr. Speaker, is in the neighbourhood of $218.
Now why should not this parliament say to the Bell Telephone Company:	You must
not issue this stock at par, but you must sell it at the market price or at some other price which will bring into the treasury of the company a large addition to your capital.

I rise to a point of order, Mr .Speaker. I understand that, under the rules which govern private bills, any private bill which is under discussion when the hour for discussion of private bills expires goes to the bottom of the list. The bill now before the House was under discussion on Wednesday evening last at 11 o'clock, when the special time allotted to private bills that evening had expired. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the same rule which governs private bills on Tuesdays and Fridays should apply also on a special occasion such as Wednesday evening, especially when as in this case the bill now before the house occupied the entire three hours on Wednesday evening.

of the fiscal year, both extensions on the same terms as originally. I have a memorandum covering the agreement with Reuters in the matter of publicity. If the committee is anxious to have it I can read it.

During 1927, 4,260 separate news items were sent by cable or mail direct to Great Britain for distribution by Reuters to practically every British publication, as well as for re-transmission, where the news interest justified, to continental and other news agencies. The total number of cabled items was 2,203, of which 624 dealt directly with^matters of trade and industrial development in Canada. These items included also the speeches of H. R. H. the Prince of Wales and Premier Baldwin during their Canadian visit, and which constituted the very best possible advertising for Canada. The total cable wordage was 155.748, or approximately 18.000 words in excess of contract requirements. The mail wordage, covering semi-weeklv budgets of news and trade items to Great Britain and monthly budgets to the overseas dominions of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and India, totalled nearly 500,000 words. This mail service was distributed, through Reuters, to every leading newspaper in Great Britain and the overseas dominions. A special weekly cable letter was sent, averaging approximately 600 words, dealing especially with a review of Canadian trade and commercial conditions, and this weekly review went to all Reuter subscribers, and also to all Canadian trade agents abroad and to a large list of complimentary recipients designated by the Canadian High Commissioner's office in London.
All important government bulletins dealing with crop reports, employment conditions, immigration statistics and financial and trade matters were cabled to London in sufficient detail to meet all requirements of official Canadian representatives overseas and thus save the expense which previously obtained of special departmental forwarding by cable of these reports.

While I am on my feet I would also suggest to the minister that he urge the Board of Grain Commissioners to give careful consideration to the question of grading garnet wheat. Up to the present time the board have ruled that garnet wheat is not eligible to be graded No. 1 northern, but I think the evidence given before the agriculture committee by the Dominion cerealist goes to show that garnet wheat is equal in quality to marquis wheat, so I think it is time it became eligible to be graded No. 1 northern. I think too much propaganda has been carried on in this country to discourage farmers from growing anything but marquis wheat, because there are some districts that are entirely unsuited to that wheat. Because of that fact and because farmers have stuck to marquis wheat in districts to which it was not suited, we have had a great deal of low grade wheat during late years. They should be allowed to grow the wheat best adapted to their particular locality. I think it must be admitted that we cannot expect one variety of wheat to be suitable all over the large area now devoted to the growing of wheat in western Canada. I think garnet wheat is very suitable in many localities, and if it is equal in quality to marquis wheat it is to be regretted that the Board of Grain Commissioners have not allowed it to be graded No. 1 northern,
I would like to bring another matter to the attention of the minister; I refer to the necessity for providing more commodious quarters for the use of the grain inspector at Calgary. I have been in there several times during the busy season when I have found fifteen or twenty men in that one little room, two men actually grading wheat, several assistants helping them and a great many grain men looking after their car samples. The place is altogether too small; this is a very important matter and I think we could afford to provide bettei quarters for the grain inspectors. I would also suggest that we need more than two inspectors at Calgary; after all, the grading of wheat is largely a matter of opinion, and I do not think it wise that two men should have to grade 500 cars of wheat in one day. They cannot give it the time it really requires. The additional expense involved in providing one or two other inspectors at that point would be a mere bagatelle.
I would ask the minister to interest himself in the question of the interchange of inspectors

between different inspection points. In the past we have had one inspector stationed at Calgary for several years at a time; he was never out of that office during the grading season except for meals and to sleep, and never had another inspector to consult with except possibly the chief inspector, who paid him a visit on an average of once a year. If we are ever to get away from a lot of dissatisfaction which now exists in connection with the grading of grain it must be done by securing uniformity in the grading system, and I do' not think we can do that in any better way than by an interchange of inspectors between Calgary, Winnipeg and Fort William. If the inspectors at Calgary were allowed to have two weeks at Winnipeg and two weeks at Fort William during the busy season, while some men from Fort William or Winnipeg took their places at Calgary, I think it would go a long way in securing uniformity in the grading carried on at these points. I would also suggest that the inspectors at some of the terminal elevators at Fort William be sent to Winnipeg and other prairie points and that inspectors from those points take the vacant places at Fort William for a month or so at a time. If possible we would like to see the wheat which is graded out of the terminals at Fort William equal to the average of the grades at the initial inspection points. We are told that that is impossible, but the board should endeavour to come as near to it as possible, and I think that cannot be done in a better way than by an interchange of these inspectors. This will involve some small expense, but I am sure the benefits which would accrue from such an interchange would more than pay for the expense involved. There have been seasons in the past when a good deal of the wheat shipped by the farmers graded one grade higher at Winnipeg than at some other point, and that is what has caused so much dissatisfaction which I am sure the minister is anxious to overcome.
I only ask him that he impress this upon the Board of Grain Commissioners because they always say that it will cost a good deal, and they would have to secure the consent of the department. I feel sure that if the minister would assure the board that they could have the extra money to pay travelling expenses, the committee would gladly vote the additional sum required. It has been said that the inspectors would object, but I am sure [DOT] they would be glad to have the opportunity of securing this added experience, and I am confident that the members of this committee would vote them the money for travelling expenses and pocket money which would compensate them for being away from home for three or four weeks during the rush season. Personally I think this is a very important matter, and I hope the minister will assure the board that as far as the expense is concerned they need not be deterred from at least making this experiment of exchanging the inspectors.

I can assure my hon.
friend that my attitude towards this act and the administration expenses involved is that it is of interest only to the producers of grain, because it is paid for by them. Parliament provides the money and the producer pays what parliament provides, in the way of fees.
Regarding the quality of grading on garnet wheat, I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the agriculture committee, now studying a reference to it on grain grading, might very well express the views of that committee on this subject to the house. I shall be very glad to give my advice to the Board of Grain Commissioners, and I am very glad to take advice from men in this house who are interested in the grain business, and who are actual producers. We look on this act as a measure to be administered for the interests of the producers and we are guided at all times by what the producers want.
As to the quarters at Calgary not being adequate, I shall be very glad to bring that to the attention of the board.
The question of the interchange of inspectors involves taking the inspectors away from home and paying their upkeep, because they will have to be quartered in the places they are sent to. Whether or not that is a justifiable expense, I think, after all, remains pretty much with the people who pay the expenses, in the form of fees, that is, the producers. I am very glad to have my hon. friend's opinion, because it has always been represented to me that the advantages in the exchange of inspectors would not be commensurate with the expense involved. I see the point that my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) is trying to make. An inspector who has probably spent all his life in the inspection of grain at Calgary might not appreciate the grading of grain as it is done at the head of the lakes or at Winnipeg. If he had a broader outlook on the grades from various areas he might be a better inspector when he returned home. On the other hand, that man might become a specialist regarding the particular districts he was in, and he might know exactly what he could get for the grades from that district. He might be a better inspector, by virtue of his length of service in that particular district, than if he came there from some other district where

different conditions obtained. I shall be glad to take that matter up with the board, and if the house feels that the additional expense involved in exchanging these men from the head of the lakes to the prairie points is to the general advantage of the producers, I shall be glad to recommend it.

I am not sure that the producers as such have decided that such a move would be advantageous. Uniformity in grading would be undoubtedly a very desirable thing to secure, but I can see where the lack tof uniformity that might result at a given point through the interchange of inspectors would be just as much to be deplored as the lack of uniformity between two given points, say Calgary and Winnipeg. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Macleod has merely been expressing his own personal opinion in regard to that matter. I am not sure that any committee or any organized body has ever pome to the conclusion that such an interchange would be desirable. Any result by -way of benefit that might be secured from such an interchange is highly problematical at the present time. If it were once determined that such a change would be beneficial and advantageous to the producer, and would bring about greater uniformity in grading, the matter of expense would be entirely a secondary consideration. For myself I have not yet been convinced that such an interchange is desirable.

I might tell the hon.
member for Lisgar that several of the points taken up by the hon. member for Macleod are now under discussion in the agriculture committee. If this point is discussed in the agriculture committee, I should like to have the guidance of those particularly interested in the administration of the act.

The subcommittee is considering some of the points mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod. He is a member of that committee, and I think the proper way to do would be to allow that committee to come to a conclusion before presenting it in this house.

While I have no objection whatever to the printing and publication of the map referred to by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar), showing the protein content of wheat in the different parts of the west, we must all bear in mind that the protein content of wheat during the past year has been very unusual. It was not a normal year and it will not give a correct idea of the protein content of wheat in a normal year. It

would be well for the minister to bear in mind that we should have a map of that kind printed from year to year for the information of the growers of wheat, and I think a certam amount should be laid aside every year for the production of a map of this kind.
Hear, hear.

I want to draw the minister's attention to something that was brought out in the agriculture committee regarding the inspection of grain at our transfer houses on the lakes. Both our commissioners and our inspectors hinted that there might be a certain amount of mixing done in these transfer houses, in fact they told us that they thought there was some mixing done. Mixing is legal, and is allowed to be done at Fort William and at our private elevators there, but once the wheat is graded, and it is never graded again, mixing should not be allowed. It would be well for the minister to take the matter up with his commissioners, or with those who are looking after the grading of wheat, with a view to seeing that proper inspectors are put at these lake ports and 'transfer houses in order to prevent mixing.

I think I would go farther than that. Not only would I put proper inspectors down there, but I would have these people forbidden to do any mixing whatever in those transfer houses. The inspection certificate has already been given when it is graded out from Fort William, and I do not think anyone should be allowed to mix grain in the transfer houses. You will have to have somebody there to watch that it is not mixed, but we certainly should not allow it to be done.

This same thing may occur again and again. Would it not be wise to have this 'laboratory installed in a building by itself?

At present the laboratory is in the Grain Exchange building, which is a convenient location for all those in the grain business. It is very convenient for the inspection and distribution of samples. The question of erecting a building to take care of this work has 'been put before us, but after looking into it we found that the expense involved, as well as the inconvenience of loca-

tion, did not justify it. Therefore we did not recommend it to the house, but rather recommended the enlarging and the perfecting of the offices in the present quarters.

I have a few points I should like to mention to the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). He lives in a district where I presume all the grain is shipped to and graded at the same point year after year. In the district in which I live, possibly half o<ur wheat is shipped west and half shipped east. Very often when we ship several cars, knowing it is all the same kind of wheat, the cars going west get a different grade from those going to Winnipeg. It got so bad in one year, I think 1925-I am only speaking from memory-that the farmers held a meeting in one of the towns in my constituency to discuss this very matter, and they passed a resolution stating that they would not ship any wheat west until the grading system at Calgary was remedied. Several farmers there stated that they were willing to take their affidavit that they had taken a sample of wheat, sent one-half of it to Winnipeg and the other half to Calgary, and that in every case the sample sent to Calgary received a grade lower than the sample sent to Winnipeg. Those of us who have had this experience have become firmly convinced that we should have an interchange of inspectors. By the time an inspector has had a month's experience of Winnipeg grading with perhaps fifteen or twenty other inspectors and has had a week's experience at Fort William he will have seen the grade that the great percentage of wheat in western Canada is receiving. He may have been used to grading only Alberta wheat, which is after all of a different type from the bulk of the wheat shipped through Winnipeg. In some of the grades of wheat there is a difference between the average sample at Calgary and at Winnipeg of seven pounds to the bushel, and a man who is grading that heavy wheat all the time is very apt to become more severe in fixing the grade than a man at Winnipeg would be. That is why we are asking for an interchange of inspectors. As long as we are in the position where one-half of our wheat is being graded say at Calgary and the other half at Winnipeg, we see the result of the lack of uniformity, and it is necessary to endeavour to do away with the dissatisfaction which exists in the minds of the farmers in regard to the grading system. We should at least make a trial of an interchange of inspectors to see whether that would bring about more uniformity than we have at the present time.
I do not see how we are going to find out what the effect will be, whether it will do any good or not, unless we try it out. I do not see how it can do any harm. I wish to thank the minister for the very fair way in which he has referred to the matter, and I assure him that the great majority of farmers in Alberta at any rate are very anxious to see this given a trial. We firmly believe that it would help to do away with the discrepancy which often exists between the grading at Calgary and Edmonton and the grading at Winnipeg. In one season, not the one to which I referred before, the grading at one of the western points was so much lower than at Winnipeg and they had so many complaints that I understand the chief inspector went out there and Stayed a week in an endeavour to get the grading of that office cm a par with the grading which was being done at Winnipeg.

The efforts in western Canada seems to be to select a rust-proof wheat and many varieties have been propagated with that end in view. Some of these give very good yields but they have not the quality of marquis or red fyfe wheat. I find that Bill No. 188 provides for a number of other grades like these varieties so that each will have its intrinsic value, but I should like to point out that if these softer wheats are mixed with the harder varieties at Fort William or Port Arthur, the price of No. 1 northern, No. 2 northern, will be still lower in the markets of the world, particularly in Great Britain where it is brought into competition with wheats from other parts of the world. I should like to know if some means will be taken to prevent these other varieties from being mixed with No. 1 and No. 2 northern at Fort William or Portt Arthur.
