Will the minister say why
an inspection point has been established at Moose Jaw and who asked for it?

I have not the information in front of me, because it is not a subject that comes up ordinarily, but there was a considerable demand for it and there is a considerable demand now for further inspection in Saskatchewan. The Minister of Agriculture has, I think, the correspondence with reference to the matter and he had the correspondence with reference to the establishment of a point at Moose Jaw. It all came up before I was in charge of the department.

I know something of the history of the establishment of an inspection point at Moose Jaw. For some fifteen years the people of the southern part of Saskatchewan, the southeastern part of Alberta and that part of the country north and west of Moose Jaw have been agitating for an inspection point there. That agitation finally came to the House of Commons; meetings were held by several members from western Canada along with the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, and it was decided to establish a grain inspection point at Moose Jaw, Finally, that grain inspection point was established last year. The results have been very satisfactory to all the people in that part of the country. A good deal of grain has been inspected there during the past year, and practically all the united farmer organizations in the country are asking that that inspection be extended at the present time. The wheat pool of Saskatchewan have had all their grain passing through Moose Jaw inspected at the Moose Jaw point, and they have made the statement on more than one occasion that it has been of great value to them, and that they have been saved a considerable amount of money through having that grading done at the inspection point in Moose Jaw. The inspection there is a. safeguard against the grain being unloaded into the elevators at the lakes before reinspection can be made. With the faster movement of grain in western Canada to-day, we have found that a car may be inspected in Winnipeg, and before the report on that car can be sent back to the shipper, the car can be landed in Fort William and unloaded. It takes a very short time to move a car from Winnipeg to Fort William. But with inspection further west, the grade can be sent back to the producer or to his agent, and a reinspection can be ordered in plenty of time to have it made at Fort William. The pool have found that this has saved them a

great deal of money this year, and all those who have used the Moose Jaw point are very well satisfied with it, and are now asking that all grain passing through there shall be inspected. I believe that the farmers' organizations in Saskatchewan are asking to have the same facilities provided at Saskatoon. The Alberta pool have had practically all their grain passing through Moose Jaw inspected there, and they have had the officers of the Saskatchewan wheat pool act as their agents at that inspection point, and also act for them in the calling for reinspection.

I may say to
my hon. friend from Rosetown, on behalf of those whom I have the honour to represent and those in that area, that I have already asked, not only this year but before, that an inspection and order point be established at Saskatoon. I am fortified in that request by the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section. I would also like to say that I agree entirely with what the hon. member for Moose Jaw has just said with respect to what the pool has found at Moose Jaw. It is believed that the inspection of grain at these two points will unquestionably be of great interest to the producers in these areas. While I do not think that this is the time when we need discuss it very fully, I rise just to say that the matter has received and is receiving consideration, and I hope it will continue to receive favourable consideration by those who have finally to deal with it.

I have no
objection personally to an inspection point, compulsory or otherwise, being established at Moose Jaw, provided it applies to the grain of the Saskatchewan people, but until there has been a request from those who are the growers in Alberta I do not think it would be either wise or proper to compel growers like my hon. friend from- Macleod or my hon. friend from Acadia or myself to have our grain compulsorily inspected passing through Moose Jaw. The principle is wrong, aside altogether from the economics of it, and I submit that the minister will be well advised when taking into consideration, favourably or otherwise, the representations of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, the hon. member for Saskatoon, or anybody else, to remember that there are also other interests besides those in Saskatchewan. I have no objection whatever to the Saskatchewan producers having their grain inspected at Moose Jaw if they so wish, but so far as Alberta is concerned I think that the question must be submitted to the growers there first.

I should like to say a
word on this particular point, because it touches the very principle of the operation of the Grain Act. Whalt my hon. friend from Bow River has just said sounds very plausible until it is examined in its relationship to the practical movement and inspection of grain at the present time. If what my hon. friend says were to be the principle applied, it would also involve that those shippers from Saskatchewan who are now shipping to Vancouver would be able to demand Vancouver inspection instead of Calgary inspection. As things exist at the present time, every grain inspection point is a compulsory inspection point for all the grain passing through there, except with regard to Moose Jaw. With regard to Moose Jaw, for reasons which I need not discuss at this stage, but which the minister can and will explain, the arrangement was made to start with that the inspection there would be voluntary, but during all the years of the Calgary inspection, even prior to the years when Edmonton inspection came into use, all grain passing through Calgary was required to be inspected at Calgary. I have rather a vivid memory of its operation because there were in the early days of Calgary inspection many Saskatchewan shippers who, strange as it may seem, preferred Vancouver inspection, inspection at the port, rather than having their grain inspected at Calgary, but there was no help for them.
I submit that the principle advocated by my hon. friend from Bow River, satisfactory as it may sound, cannot work in practice unless it is universally applied, and if it were universally applied, that is, if every shipper had the right to choose the point at which his particular car should be inspected, that would undoubtedly involve very great difficulties in the matter of transportation and undoubtedly increase the cost of handling the cars. In fact, one of the arguments for changing the present system at Moose Jaw to the system which is in vogue elsewhere is that very fact-the transportation economics of the situation. Under the present system of voluntary inspection a trainload of cars comes into Moose Jaw, and half or three-quarters of' those cars are inspected at Moose Jaw. That means that the train must be split, and the remainder of the cars have to be carried on, or else the cars which need not be delayed for inspection at Moose Jaw are in fact delayed there, and delayed again at Winnipeg for the inspection which takes place there. I do not believe it will be practicable from a transportation standpoint
Supply-Canada Grain Act

very long to operate a voluntary system of inspection anywhere. If we have inspection points we must expect, as a matter of practical transportation economies, that the grain passing through those points will be inspected there. I would go this far with my hon. friend, however, that the reinspection privilege would thereby be widened1. The inspection at Moose Jaw of grain coming eastward from Alberta, to the extent that it does come eastward from Alberta, rather increases the chances of the owner of the grain on reinspection. In my own experience in the business I know that very frequently it has happened, with the speeding up of transportation in recent years, that inspections made at Winnipeg in the rush season-the rush, remember, not only in the inspection, but in the offices getting out the slips to the shippers or their agents-would involve your receiving notice that the car on which you are applying for reinspection at Port William had been unloaded before the request for reinspection arrived there, whereas inspection nearer the point of origin gives the shipper of the grain a greater length of time in which to appeal for reinspection. Surely there would be no more reason why noncompulsory inspection should be practised at Moose Jaw than that there should be compulsory inspection at Calgary, Edmonton or Winnipeg. I think the advocacy of hon. members on this side of the house and in the opposite corner of an interchange of grain inspectors is much more to the point with regard to securing uniformity of grading than any question of compulsory or non-compulsory grading at a particular point. As we look to the future we must of necessity contemplate the possibility of more points in western Canada at which inspection will be made. When the Hudson bay route opens up for traffic, there is no question about it, we must arrange some point for the inspection of grain convenient as a funnel to that route, and there is a great deal to be said in favour of inspection points both at Moose Jaw and at Saskatoon. Naturally the minister desires to go slowly in matters of this kind. I am not one of those who believe we will ever need to go outside of the present points, plus Saskatoon and some point in the future which would be the funnel for the Hudson bay line. I think those points would very naturally comply with all the requirements of western producers; I do not think there would be any necessity to ;o any wider than 
that; but I think within the next five years w'e shall reach that point where there will be inspection at Moose Jaw, Saskatoon, Hudson Bay junction, Calgary, Edmonton, and the usual terminal inspection at Winnipeg, Vancouver, Prince Rupert, and Fort William and Port Arthur.

representative of that portion of the country northwest of Moose Jaw, I can assure the minister that the farmers are looking forward with a great deal of satisfaction to Moose Jaw becoming a compulsory inspection point. We have found on many occasions, just as he has stated, that before we can get word through for reinspection the car has gone forward and it is impossible to secure reinspection. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) pointed out to the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) the very thing that I was on my feet to tell him. I happen to be situated just on the dividing line, and our wheat goes west or it goes east. If it goes west, we in that part of Saskatchewan have to submit to its being graded at Calgary. When you consider that 50 per cent of the wheat that is grown in the three prairie provinces originates in Saskatchewan, I think it will be conceded that we are at least entitled to some recognition. I am heartily behind the establishment of compulsory points both at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw.

Probably the minister could give us information as to how many cars of wheat have passed through Moose Jaw in a given season, and as to how many of those cars have been inspected, and how many have been reinspected either at Winnipeg or Fort William. I am sorry that I cannot give my hon. friend the number of cars that have passed through Moose Jaw, but about 16,000 cars were inspected there during the last crop season.

Returning for the moment, Mr. Chairman, to the Moose Jaw inspection division, the Minister of Rail-

Inspection at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw is not a good thing until you have more mechanized and made perfect the grading of grain. The more inspection points you have the more you create room for dissatisfaction and discord among the farmers as to whether they are getting fair grades or not. It has been our experience in Alberta that if we ship samples to Calgary, Edmonton and everywhere else we get entirely different grades. The same would hold true with respect to Moose Jaw and Saskatoon, and you would get into a state of hopeless confusion and the whole inspection system would be discredited.
How could that occur? If your car was inspected at Calgary westbound or at Moose Jaw eastbound, that same car would not be inspected at Winnipeg.
I was speaking of submitting samples at the various inspection points. Many farmers before shipping a car take the precaution of shipping samples. We get three or four different grades.
You get them anyway.

Yes; but why intensify the problem? Let us first improve our grading system.
Mr. 'VALLANCE: You are assuming that your one car should go through only one point. You are not eliminating the danger.

All right, I say frankly to the minister if these points are absolutely needed to protect the interests of the growers of grain, I for one will raise no objection; but I do ask him to take the greatest precaution before he brings any more new inspection points into being, especially compulsory points. We have a multiplicity of them, increasing on demand from time to time as the trade grows. There were reasons for this when the trade was growing rapidly, but there has to be a limit. I notice that the hon. member (Mr. Vallance) makes an interjection to the effect that he knows what I mean. I am so glad he got the point before I sat down.

The Minister of Agriculture has received a great many representations on behalf of the producers in Saskatchewan urging that, Moose Jaw be created an order point, which is what this means. I personally have not seen the representations, nor have I as minister, up to the present time, recommended that these various orders points be created. There is one thing that I want to say on this subject, and it is this. I believe that familiarity with grading, if the grading is properly done, does create a certain confidence in the minds of the producers; and the chairman of the board, discussing the subject with me some time ago, made the statement that there was one benefit that did accrue from voluntary inspection during the past season, and that was that the farmers themselves in great numbers were enabled to visit the place and see the inspection of their grain. As a result they did feel that they were getting good inspection. They felt a confidence in the inspectors which they did not have when the inspection was done at points further away.
I thoroughly agree with what my hon. friend from Bow River says. Personally as minister I do not want to see too many inspection points, but I do believe with the hon. member for Macleod that, with an exchange of inspectors, it is not likely that you will have a greater variety of grading at five points than at three. You are just as likely to have irregularities in the human judgment of grain in three points as in five. There is no particular reason to assume that the man you have in Moose Jaw will degrade or upgrade grain any more than the man at Winnipeg or Calgary or Vancouver. I do not believe you can possibly expect to have anything but a variety of standards if you multiply the inspection points to too great an extent. But I believe with the hon, member for Macleod that with a proper exchange you can handle all the principal points we need. And I believe with the Minister of Railways that the day will come-whether that day

has arrived or not I am not prepared to say-when we shall probably have to have an inspection point for the outlet of the funnel at Hudson bay and one or two more inspection points in Saskatchewan. Beyond that, however, I do not see any need for more points in Canada.

I think one most important
point has been entirely overlooked in connection with the multiplicity of inspection points. If you establish compulsory inspection points at all these places mentioned you will compel all the grain companies and pools to maintain agencies at those various points in order that they might have their own representatives there to inspect the grain. That means considerable expense; it means an increase in the expense of the inspection department. For these two reasons there is an objection to compulsory grading being established at Moose Jaw. There is ground for compulsory inspection at Winnipeg, Calgary and Edmonton, and when we begin to use the Hudson bay route there will have to be a compulsory point on that line. These are points outside the producing territory and they will get all the wheat that is being sent either to the head of the lakes, or to Hudson bay or to the Pacific ocean. In my judgment it is necessary to have compulsory inspection at those points, so that before the cars reach the terminal elevators the railway company will know the result in regard to each one of the cars. But on account of the expense involved to the people interested, in Moose Jaw particularly, they should be willing to go slow there in this matter. It will mean a great deal of expense, and we know by experience that all these expenses fall ultimately on the producer, and are taken out of the price of his wheat. That is the real basic objection to the establishment of more compulsory points. We cannot very well object to voluntary inspection at these points, and as a matter of fact, the interior terminal elevators are located at Moose Jaw and Saskatoon and there must be one inspector anyway at each of these places. So that no one can object to voluntary inspection there. But we should go slow about establishing too many compulsory points.

I wonder whether my
hon. friend, who has presented his argument fairly, takes into account when considering the question of expense to the grain companies, the fact that that expense goes on whether or not the inspection is compulsory. If the inspection is voluntary, the expense of maintaining the necessary men to check the

samples is just as great as if the inspection were made compulsory and all cars passing through were inspected. I know something about the cost of maintaining such a checking system and I can assure my hon. friend that the cost of infinitesimal to the grain company to maintain the checking of its grades at any point where grading is done. There is always an additional expense to the inspection department to the extent to which additional inspectors are required. One would think, to hear this discussion, that inspection at Saskatoon and Moose Jaw was a new thing. Millions of bushels have been inspected at both these places in the last number of years, particularly in seasons of off-grade crops, when both terminal elevators have been required to handle the crops and the farmers have desired inspection there. As a matter of -fact, they had to have it for their grain going into storage temporarily in the interior terminal elevators; and if you admit inspection at all, there is very little difference, in the expense to those handling the grain, as between voluntary and compulsory inspection.
My hon. friend from Wetaskiwin asked a question with respect to the pool. The best answer I can give regarding the pool's attitude towards Moose Jaw inspection is the fact that in spite of inspection at Moose Jaw being voluntary, during the last crop season the wheat pool did have all their cars passing through Moose Jaw inspected there. That is the best evidence that they are satisfied of its value to them in actual operation. My hon. friend from Last Mountain asked a question regarding the number of cars inspected there. According to the last record I saw-I do not know whether the minister has it here tonight-there have been, up to three or four months ago, some 16,000 cars inspected at that point, if memory serves me correctly. It was very widely used.

How
many oars have passed through there?

I cannot say; but my
hon. friend will bear in mind the fact that the wheat pool of Saskatchewan controls over SO per cent of the crop and all their cars were inspected there. All the cars going in that direction were inspected there. At least 50 per cent of the grain grown northwest of, southwest of and west of Moose Jaw must have been inspected there last year-because the pool controls that much-and, in addition, some at any rate of that controlled by ordinary companies in the grain trade. Not all of the ordinary grain companies but most of them
opposed that innovation, as they have opposed every innovation that has ever been made in the handling of grain since the inception of the practice.

With regard to this inspection of wheat at Moose Jaw I have been and am at present a grower of wheat to some considerable extent, and have shipped wheat from western Canada for a good many years. Most of the wheat from the constituency which I have the honour to represent goes through Moose Jaw, and the people of my constituency are anxious to have this made a compulsory grain inspection point. Of late I have received many communications both from the pool directors and others urging that this action be taken. For the life of me I cannot see why the hon. member for Macleod should be so much interested in the financial welfare of the grain trade. He thinks if Moose Jaw were made a compulsory inspection point they would have to have a man there. I have shipped grain from these points and I am not interested in whether or not they have a man there; they never send a man there unless it is to pick out a few good cars of wheat and send them wherever they please. I do not care whether or not they send a man to Moose Jaw to inspect my grain.

The reason I mentioned the
expense was not because I am interested in the grain trade but because I am interested in the Alberta pool. So long as it is voluntary I do not think it will be necessary for the Alberta pool to maintain an office to check the cars, but if you make it compulsory you will compel the Alberta pool to maintain an agency there for that purpose.

My information is that
even now, when it is voluntary, the Alberta pool is using Moose Jaw inspection.

Perhaps I might complete the remarks I want to make, now that this little talk is over. As a grower of wheat I cannot see that these men should object to some compulsion. I ship wheat east and west; every time my wheat goes through Calgary I am compelled to have it inspected there, and every time it goes through Winnipeg I am compelled to have it inspected there. I do not see why these people should object if a little of their wheat happens to dribble through Moose Jaw and they are compelled to have it inspected. That is not

The hon. member for Macleod asked regarding the inspection of Alberta pool wheat. The Minister of Railways stated that all pool cars were inspected in Moose Jaw.	All pool cars from pool
elevators are inspected in Moose Jaw, but although this house passed an act last year saying that the farmer had the right to designate where his grain should be inspected, the grain trade for which my hon. from Macleod wishes to save money-
I protest against that statement. I have already said that I am not interested in the grain trade, and I think the hon. member is not fair.

Very well; I
hope the hon. member is not interested in the grain trade.

I will withdraw
the statement, if that is what my hon. friend wants. Although this act was passed last year, the grain trade have not been following the act because when a pool farmer has to ship his grain through a line elevator, the line elevator man takes the stand that once the grain is handed over to him he has the right to say where it shall be inspected. He takes charge of the grain until it is handed over to the pool again at Fort William.

Is the hon. member
correct in stating that the amendment to the act gave the farmer the right to designate the point of inspection? Did it not rather give him the right to designate the terminal to which the grain should be shipped? That is a different matter.

That is a different matter. I did not intend to say it gave him the right to say where the grain should be inspected; I intended to say that the

act gave the farmer the right to designate to what terminal elevator it should go; it gave him the right to send his grain anywhere, but the grain trade are not following that act. Once the grain is taken into a line elevator, even though it belongs to the pool, the line elevator man claims the right to handle that grain as he sees fit until he returns it to the pool at the other end. The result is that all pool grain handled through the line elevators is inspected where the elevator man wishes it to be inspected, and though the pools may wish to have it inspected at Moose Jaw, they cannot force its inspection there.
I want to say a word with regard to the multiplicity of inspection points. I think that is an advantage at times, during the heavy run of grain. In regard to inspection anywhere, the farmer has the right to government inspection of grain, and government inspection in one place is the same as government inspection at another place; at least it should be the same, and as a general rule I believe it is the same or at least very similar at all inspection points. The amount of money it will cost the grain trade to check samples at any of these points does not amount to very much and should not be taken into consideration in view of the fact that the people producing the grain want this service in their part of the country. They have been absolutely satisfied with what they have received so far and they want compulsory inspection so that they will be able to go in and see how their grain is inspected. They want to be able to send samples into this point and have them inspected before they ship their grain, and I do not see why they should not be allowed to have that service if they desire it.

I was surprised to hear the hon. member for Bow River and the hon. member for Macleod offer such objections to further grain inspection points. I did not expect that this discussion would be precipitated on this item, but I have letters from the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, and also a letter from the pool to that same organization, saying that in their judgment the matter of inspection points in Saskatchewan is of great interest to the producers of this country.
That is the Saskatchewan pool?

Yes, and I
assume that if it is of interest to the Saskatchewan pool it is of equal interest to the

farmers who belong to the Alberta pool and who ship their grain eastward. The minister might tell
the committee something of the general scheme under which the various trade commissioners operate. There is just one complaint I have heard and1 that is that there has been indicated in one or two cases a tendency on the part of some of our agents to show much more consideration for some firms than for others engaged in the same trade. I think the minister knows exactly what I refer to. What can be done to meet that situation?

I am informed by my
deputy that we have not a single complaint of that kind on the files of the department, or it would be investigated. But as I said a moment ago, I think it is only the logical thing to suppose that if an aggressive firm sends its representative out into a certain field and he asks our man there to assist him in giving him introductions to possible buyers of some Canadian product, our man in the field, being human, will try to support that firm which is aggressive enough to send its representative out in an effort to develop business. I do not believe that there is any genuine complaint that our men in the field

have shown any partiality, but naturally they have shown a great willingness to help those who have gone to the foreign field. We have at the present time so many unsolicited favourable comments on the work that has been done by our commissioners that any criticism I might have to offer as minister of the department would seem infinitesimal in comparison with the compliments I would wish to pay to our men in the field.

Would the minister give
roughly the salaries that are paid to these trade commissioners?

The salaries range from
15,760, with a living allowance of $2,000, which is paid to one of our senior men, Mr. Ross, in Melbourne, down to salaries of $2,040, with a living allowance of $1,500.
The highest is $7,760.
Yes, that is received by our commissioners in Melbourne, London and Calcutta-salary, $5,760, living allowance, $2,000.

On page ZZ-20 of the
Auditor General's report, under the vote for the commercial intelligence service, I find an item of $4,298.63 for advertising in various newspapers and periodicals. What is the explanation of that?

I am informed by my
deputy that this covers the small advertisements that may be inserted in local newspapers from time to time giving notification of the location of our offices. There are twenty-four offices included in that amount of $4,000 odd. It is not a publicity vote at all.	.
